speechtext: Hon. H. H. STEVENS (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 9, to amend the Canada Grain Act.

speechtext: Explain, please.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a condition prevails in the country well known to all hon. members. Commodity prices have fallen but the charges incident to such commodities have not in all cases fallen to a corresponding degree. The government has been studying
Questions

this situation with a view to lessening the burden placed upon the farmer by the movement of grain, and it has been found necessary to secure an amendment to the act in order to achieve this purpose. This bill is to amend section 134 of the act by adding the words "except by order or regulation of the board."
A full description or analysis of the situation can be given at a later stage of the bill.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege. A few days ago I visited your office along with the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) and showed you a document on the strength of which I proposed to move the adjournment of this house in order to debate a question of urgent public importance. This matter concerned the financial position of the Sun Life Assurance Company and the conduct of a senior official. Your Honour told me that I would have your permission to make use of the document in full, and when I again visited your office accompanied by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer), Your Honour repeated that I would have permission to make a statement on the floor of the house but that you would then rule against my proceeding with the motion as the matter was not one of recent occurrence. I then asked if I could have permission to treat it as a notice of motion, and you told me there was nothing in the rules to prevent that, I could put the entire
document on the order paper by way of a notice of motion. After the vote in this house on your ruling I sent the document to the clerk of the house by way of notice of motion. I was asked to modify it slightly, which I did, and I was then informed that the matter would appear in votes and proceedings of Thursday. When I received my copy of votes and proceedings on Thursday I found that it did not contain my notice of motion. Upon getting in touch with the clerk's office I was informed that through some mistake this notice had not been put in, but that it would be in today's votes and proceedings. Upon receiving my copy today I find that my notice is not included. Is some official of this house exceeding his authority or is there some powerful influence at work to conceal from the people of Canada the true situation in connection with the Sun Life? I make that statement because on Wednesday Your Honour stated that the rules of the house provided other opportunities for discussing this matter but my endeavours to avail myself of those opportunities have not been successful. I have been denied that privilege and I ask for some explanation.

On the orders of the day:
Hon. II. H. STEVENS (Minister of Trade and Commerce): The other day the hon. mem-

ber for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth) asked me when we might expect census figures relative to unemployment to be released. I replied that I understood a considerable portion of those figures had already been released and that I would advise him as soon as possible of the progress being made.
A bulletin showing the number of unemployed, male and female, as of date June 1, 1931, in cities and towns of 5,000 and over, was issued last April. In addition this was published in full in the Labour Gazette, the official journal of the Labour department. There is now being issued this month a further bulletin extending the figures to places of 1,000 and over, and giving the totals for the whole of Canada by provinces, differentiating by sex, and showing the causes of unemployment. This statement will be available about the middle of next week. These figures were ready some weeks ago but some last minute checking is found advisable to see that they are as accurate as possible.
In addition to the general summary above mentioned we have ready for the printer a series of about twenty bulletins on individual cities of 30,000 and over which will review the situation in full detail. I might add that the study of this subject will comprise some six or eight volumes, quite a number at all events, exhaustively analyzing the figures and the facts in connection with the situation. The preparation of this final summary is now well advanced, but it will be some little time yet before it will be issued. But the bulletin issued in April last is a fairly complete bulletin dealing with towns of 5,000 and over, which really comprise the major portion of the figures desired.
I should like to indicate to the house that the compilation of this data naturally takes some time, and I do not think there is the slightest reason to complain of the work done by the bureau in this regard. I am convinced, as far as I can judge from very close contact with the facts, that their work in this respect has been very commendable. I should not like the impression to be left that there was the slightest degree of neglect by the bureau in the production of these figures.

speechtext: I would like to submit to my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce that I doubt very much if he will get an accurate figure of the unemployment in this dominion by limiting the scope of the calculations to towns of 1,000. Canada, as my hon. friend knows, has never in the past had any machinery for computing unemployment figures, and we have always based our calculations on the number of men gainfully employed; comparing that index figure with the index figure of a previous day we can make a rough calculation of the number of unemployed by ascertaining how many fewer men are gainfully employed today. The greatest problem in unemployment, of course, always arises where men are gathered in the large centres of population, and where as a mass they are more difficult to take care of and' find employment for than in the smaller communities. But the fact is true that a great many of those who are unemployed in the Dominion of Canada have returned to the rural parts of the country and are now living back in the small villages and on the farms whence they came. In my opinion they are doing the wisest thing possible to relieve the unemployment situation by trying to act as good citizens in their own towns or on the farms, thereby not aggravating the unemployment situation in the large centres. I am of the opinion that a census of the rural parts of the province of Ontario, including the smaller villages, would reveal that there is very substantial unemployment represented by this class of citizen, who is causing no very great problem, but is nevertheless out of work. If our figures of unemployment are to be accurate to allow us to gauge the necessities of the situation, I submit to the minister that it would be wise to have a calculation of the number so unemployed.

That the dominion control of currency and credit should be so exercised as to provide and maintain sufficient purchasing power to;

And that the issue of this currency and credit should be based upon the natural wealth and productive capacity of this country, not, as at the present time, upon one single commodity, gold, and that its volume should be determined by the goods and services to be dealt with, and the legitimate requirements of the people;
This house is further of opinion, that this step should be taken in the immediate future, pending other fundamental changes, and as an integral part of a system of planned economy,



The Address-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
which is becoming generally recognized as essential, in order that the natural wealth and productive energy of this country may be utilized to provide a satisfactory standard of living for all our people.
Mr. Speaker, the necessity for a motion of that kind must ibe apparent to hon. members who will examine the actual internal conditions of the country. If they will study the effects of unemployment and declining price levels they will be able to make a fairly accurate estimate of the decline in income brought about by unemployment and underemployment in industry. Taking the average wage in the dominion as around SI,000, and estimating the total on the basis of the number of unemployed we find that the loss of income in the term of three years is about
SI,320,000,000. There is that much money less with which to purchase goods produced or possible of production by Canadian industry.
Concerning agriculture even more accurate estimates are available. The gross agricultural revenue for the year 1929 was $1,631,081,000; by 1930 it had fallen to $1,262,047,000; by 1931 it had fallen to 8880,240,000. It is still falling rapidly. From figures available in the Bureau of Statistics we now find that there is a difference in the purchasing power of the farmer in 1930 over 1929 of $369,000,000, in 1931 over 1929 of $880,000,000 and in 1932 over 1931 of $800,000,000, or a total of over $2,000,000,000. In order to avoid any error in calculation and to make sure that overlapping is avoided, for the sake of being conservative in my figures I am willing to cut that figure in two, and to assume that the farmers have suffered a loss in income of only $1,000,000,000.
Now let us consider the condition of the earning classes, the salaried and professional people in the community. In connection with these people also we have means whereby we may make a fairly accurate estimate. The income tax returns supply us with that information. I do not think any hon. member will deny that in 1930 and 1931 the incomes of salaried and professional classes declined at least 20 per cent, and in the following year by 30 per cent. During the past two and three-quarter years it is fair to conclude that the incomes of individuals in Canada must have been depreciated to the extent of about $675,000,000.
We add up the three sums, namely, the $1,325,000,000 as a result of unemployment and under employment, the $1,000,000,000 for loss of income in agriculture, and the $675,000,000 lost by other individuals and we have a grand total of approximately $3,000,000,000. That, in short, is what the depression

has cost Canada, and the condition towards the correction of which the policy of this administration should be directed. So far they have failed to take any adequate steps in that direction for reasons I can quite readily understand. To check the continued destruction of business and continued unemployment requires not the patching of the competitive system but the institution of an entirely new economic and social order.

Hon. members opposite are inclined to laugh at facts such as I have stated. All right, I call to my support as witness one of the most eminent bankers of the British Empire, Sir Basil Blackett, director of the Bank of England. If hon. members will turn to Who's Who they will find who he is. Not only is he a director of that bank, but he is chairman of the Imperial and International Communications Limited, secretary to the Indian Finance and Currency Commission, and to the Capital Issues Committee of 1915. In October of 1914 he went on a special mission to the United States government in connection with exchange problems arising out of the war. He was a member of the National War Savings Committee, and representative of the British treasury in the United States from 1917 to 1919. This is a man whose reputation and respectability is beyond reproach. What does he say? In his last lecture before the Halley Stewart Institute of Great Britain as published in a book entitled The World's Economic Crisis by Salter, Stamp, Keynes, Blackett, Clay and Beveridge, his words appear at page 98 as follows:
I wish to put before you this evening the view that conscious corporative planning is not only a desirable means of progress but an unavoidable necessity-
Note the words, "unavoidable necessity"-
-if we are to save the economic structure of modern civilization from disaster.
Then, two pages later on, he calls upon the support of the Prince of Wales. Commenting upon a statement by the Prince of Wales, Sir Basil Blackett has this to say:
The Prince of Wales was calling for planned social effort by the individual, and it is significant that his emphasis was laid on the fact that such social effort has to be consciously organized and planned if it is to be of any use to the community.
Then, again at page 105 of the same document, having pointed out that in the forefront of the reforms which a planned

The Address-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
twentieth century demands is a stable money whose purchasing power will remain constant, he has this to say:
It is to our failure to seize this primary necessity of any rational monetary system that our present distress is preeminently to be attributed.
Not only are the facts I have recited concerning the condition of agriculture, unemployment and business ascertainable in these statistics supplied by the bureau, but we know from our own knowledge how desperate conditions really are. For example, how much longer can we expect the farmers to carry on when not only are the receipts from wheat and live stock below the cost of production, but the receipts from the products of mixed farming, that branch of agriculture which we were advised so strongly to go. into, have taken a similar fall.
In a letter from a farmer in the northern part of the province of Alberta, it is stated that it took four dozen eggs to buy a spool of white and a spool of black thread-four dozen eggs to buy two spools of thread. It took four dozen eggs to buy a cake of laundry soap and one of toilet soap. Two and a half dozen were required to get a box of matches, ten dozen to get a pound of tea, and two and a half dozen for a tin of pepper. To be fair, we follow this out and find that in the case of the manufacturer it takes many times more boxes of paper, many times more spools of thread to meet investment charges and overhead.

I have before me a part of the report of the central board of the British Cooperative Union to the sixty-fourth congress of the union at Glasgow, dated May 16-18, 1932. I use this quotation to demonstrate what others besides Lord Marley, Messrs. Keynes, Kitson and others have to say about this matter; they believe that the present order must undergo a drastic change. The report reads as follows:
Capitalist apologists cannot explain in terms which do not condemn their theory the disconcerting fact that, at the apex of productive capacity, world consumption and exchange of commodities are dwindling. Systematic destruction of valuable goods alleged to have been over-produced, the collapse of credit systems sanctified by banking tradition, and reversions to crude barter reveal even to the man in the street the lamentable failure of competitive industry and the flimsiness of its foundations. In such a world of unreality the simple verities of the cooperative ideal stand out as basic common sense.
We now find hon. members of the _ Conservative party taking a position which is not only antisocial and unintelligent but in direct variance with the policies preached and pronounced by just as sincere Tories in other lands. For example, I have before me an editorial which appeared in Lord Beaver-brook's Journal, the Daily Express, under date of Wednesday, April 13. It reads as follows:
The time is long overdue for a reversal-and a dramatic reversal of the monetary policy of Great Britain.
We have asked for that in this country for many years. The editorial continues:
The national need is for a steady expansion of credit facilities. The Bank of England is the obstacle in the way of that need, and because of its vested power it has imposed upon the government for ten years a policy of deflation.
Let me interject here a few remarks. I say to those who hold up the bogey of inflation to frighten the people that this country and most countries of the world have always been happier, better off and more prosperous on a measured and reasonable inflation than under deflation. I say to them furthermore that I defy them to demonstrate intelligently or logically in this house or any other place how they are going to restore industrial prosperity without inflation. We cannot continue with
the present price levels; debts cannot be paid, our own people and country are going into bankruptcy. We must have rising price levels and new activity, and we cannot have those without inflation. It must be remembered that no hon. member in this corner has ever urged the wild and stupid policies of rabid, uncontrolled inflation which have been pursued by desperate governments under desperate conditions; what we seek is a managed and intelligent inflation, an inflation which has a definite basis and a distinct regard for price levels and the quantities of goods to be consumed. It is the negation of intelligence to say that men do not exist or that bodies cannot be created that will have the power and intelligence to control such a policy. I should like to continue with Lord Beaverbrook's editorial, and I call the following to the attention of hon. members:
In other words, the Bank of England, which owes no responsibility to the electorate, dictates the government's financial policy.
The system is definitely wrong. It has played an enormous part in bringing about the postwar economic distress, and the men who conducted the bank's affairs then are still in charge.
It is no use tinkering with the question of reform. The present situation should be brought to an end.
The government must be master in its own house; the government must dictate the nation's monetary policy; and the Bank of England must be relegated to its rightful place as the servant of the nation.
If I could paraphrase by substituting for the words "the Bank of England" the words "the banks of Canada," or to be still more candid, "the federal reserve system of 'the United States" I would repeat word for word as part of my policy those words of Lord Beaverlbrook which appeared in the Daily Express. We must have control of our banking system. We can no longer leave that to the haphazard and foolish judgment of private individuals who, driven solely by the profit motive, have so jeopardized the whole existence of this so-called civilization and have brought it to a point where a new order is imperative. I simply repeat the words of the director of the Bank of England, whom I already quoted.
All along the line we have simultaneously to get to work to overhaul existing methods and practices and to rebuild our institutions. In the economic sphere agriculture, marketing, transport, housing, all need attention in close coordination with each other, and all have to be interrelated with the social services, with health services, with education, with the problem of provision for our leisured hours.
The same gentleman, having pursued much the same course as I have in depicting what

In his concluding paragraph, Sir Basil Blackett uses these words, which I call to your attention, Mr. Speaker, and to the attention of hon. members opposite with all the earnestness at my command:
For the first time in human history the mere problem of daily subsistence lias ceased to be the primary pre-occupation of a large part of the inhabitants of the earth. There is no reason why in a short time any human being should feel serious anxiety about the provision of food and clothing and houseroom for himself and for those for whom he is responsible. Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata):	Mr. Speaker, as I have very little
time after perusing official publications, I must apologize for not being more familiar with the theories and systems of so many economists. Inflation might be interesting when considered theoretically, but although I am a poor man, I cannot believe in such a policy. I have a dollar in my pocket. It may be. It may be rubbish in accordance with theories that have not yet been applied. If the economists should meet together and concentrate their theories, forming one system instead of as many systems as there are individuals, then one might learn the practical result that might ensue from those systems. But until this is done, one may be allowed to be a little doubtful about the matter, although I do not challenge the good faith of my hon. friend who is always interesting when he delivers a speech in the house.
Yesterday a challenge was issued by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), to every member of the House of Commons. May I refer to those explicit statements that were made during the campaign of 1930. At Cornwall, on June 27, the leader of the Conservative party said:
We propose at the first session of parliament to effect such legislation as will give Canadians (Mr. E. J. Garland ]
fair opportunity in competition with any country in the world. I will enact such tariff measures to give Canadians an even chance, or perish in the attempt. At the same time we will protect labour as well as consumers. There will be no exploitation.
The Prime Minister should be labelled as perishable. This is his declaration in regard to our blasting our way into the markets of the world. At Victoria, on June 17, he said, as reported in the Victoria Colonist of the same date:
It is true we must have foreign markets, and as I said the other evening we will blast a way to those markets on a world-wide basis with any exportable surpluses. We do not have to worry about that.
At Vancouver on June 18, as reported in the Province of that date, he said:
If Mr. Mackenzie King thinks I will not so build up our agricultural and industrial life that its strength will drive our products into the markets of the world, then he is wrong. For that I will do. If he thinks I will not establish new markets for these products, strive with all my heart to retain them, drive our products with all my power into new markets, into old markets, into reluctant markets, he is wrong. For that I will do.
After the election, on September 16, 1930, the Prime Minister made this statement as reported on page 238 of Hansard of that date:
He said: Mr. Speaker, in moving that you do now leave the chair, I do so because of the disturbed conditions that exist in this country and because of the circumstances that this parliament has been called to consider the problem of unemployment. I indicated a few days ago that the measures proposed were three in number, of which a tariff measure was one. Our tariff measure is not a general revision of the tariff, but deals only with such items in the tariff as it is believed will ensure additional employment to a large number of men and women in Canada.
Then he continues:
It is not for the purposes of protection that the tariff is being revised today.
He did not say "increased"; he said "revised." That was a euphemism. The tariff board had been dispensed with and the right hon. gentleman himself was revising the tariff without any other assistance. He continued :
The resolutions that are being submitted to this house are not for the purpose of affording protection in the sense in which that term is usually used; but if that term is used to designate just what we, during the election, indicated that it did mean, namely, the giving to Canadians an equality of opportunity with others who are building up their country to enable us to build up our dominion, and to give fair competition to the worker in Canada, be it man or woman, then it is protection that we

The Address

Mr. Pouliot
propose. Tliere can be no doubt, Mr. Speaker, in the mind of any hon. gentleman within sound of my voice that this government at least has a mandate to give effect to that policy.
That was true, but it was an experiment.
In every part of this dominion I was at great care to make it known to the audiences who listened to what I had to say, so that there could be no mistake as to what I meant, that in the event of their supporting candidates of our party they thereby supported a policy that -would ensure fair competition to Canadian workmen and workwomen and equality of opportunity to Canadians to build up their country.
He continues:
A number of items only will be dealt with. They will be dealt with on the basis of the employment that will be given to those who ' are not now unemployed. And we have very definite assurances from the producers in this country that as a result of the action we are taking they will increase the number of men and women in their mills and factories. I said the other day, Mr. Speaker, that the number might be estimated at 25,000 within a reasonable time.
I think that is too low an estimate, but I desired that the estimate should be at least conservative-as in keeping with the party for which I speak at this moment. When I say
25,000,	I think I am understating the number of men and women who will find employment by reason of the action that we are taking.
This is the last quotation from the observations of the present Prime Minister on that occasion:
We propose therefore to provide that so far as may be reasonably possible the requirements of the 10,000,000 people living on the northern half of this continent shall be provided by Canadian producers.
This was said during the special session on September 16, 1930. There is no excuse for poverty, as the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) has said, but there is a reason for it. The government tried an experiment by raising the tariff. These are the results, and the figures will give the house an idea of the logic of the Liberal party and of the lack of logic of the Conservative party. In 1930, the total Canadian imports were $1,248,000,000, a decrease of $17,000,000 from the preceding year. The exports were $1,144,000,000, a decrease of $243,000,000 from the preceding year. That decrease includes a decrease of S147,000,000 of exports to the United Kingdom. This explains why the Liberal government of that day submitted to the house and to the country a scheme of British preference. They wanted to increase the British preference in order to retain such a good client and to keep the trade going. After the present government had raised the
tariff during the special session, Canadian imports in 1931 amounted to $906,000,000, a decrease of $341,000,000 from the preceding year. The Prime Minister was blasting his way into the markets of the world and the result was a decrease of $341,000,000 in imports alone. Has he any reason to say now: "We have succeeded where others have failed?" The total Canadian exports in 1931 amounted to $816,000,000, or a decrease of $328,000,000 from 1930. The Prime Minister was blasting our trade into the markets of the world, and every time he blasted, the hole became deeper. Did he have any reason in 1931 to say, "We have succeeded where others have failed"? In 1932 our total Canadian imports were $578,000,000, a decrease of S328,000,000 over the preceding year. The Prime Minister was blasting, and again the hole became deeper. But he nevertheless continued to follow the same policy. Did he have any reason then to say, "We have succeeded where others failed"? In the same year, 1932, the total Canadian exports were $587,000,000, a decrease of $229,000,000 over the preceding year. The Prime Minister was blasting and the hole again became deeper. Did he have any reason there to say, "We have succeeded where others have failed"?
Here are the figures of the total decrease in Canadian trade for the two years ending March 31, 1932. The total decrease in imports was $669,000,000 or 53-7 per cent, and the total decrease in exports was $557,000,000 or 48-7 per cent. The Prime Minister was blasting our trade, and the hole became deeper and deeper.
At times we hear something said about a favourable balance of trade. If one buys nothing and sells only one cent's worth, one has a favourable balance of trade. It reminds me of the story of two old friends vho met. Paul asked Joe, "What is your business?" Joe replied, "I have a very good business." "What is it," his friend asked. "I am selling clay pipes," Joe replied. "Do you make much money at that?" asked Paul. "Oh, yes" said Joe. "How much do you pay for them, and what is your profit?" Paul asked. "I buy them for one cent, and sell them for one cent." "Then where is your profit?" Paul asked. "Oh," Joe replied, "a few may break occasionally." I think that story applies very well to the understanding of trade by the government, and especially by the Prime Minister.
May I submit some figures from the official report of the Department of Trade and
The Address-Mr. Pouliot

Commerce for the year ending March 31,
1931,	showing Canada's decrease in trade with different countries?
With the United Kingdom our trade was $368,000,000. The Prime Minister was blasting our trade in 1930 and in 1931, and the decrease with one country in one year was $102,000,000. Did he have any reason to say "We have succeeded where others have failed"?
With the United States our trade was

With the British Empire our trade in that year was $407,000,000. The Prime Minister was still blasting our trade, and with what result? A hole of $134,000,000. Did he have any reason to say, "We have succeeded where others have failed"?
With foreign countries our trade was
81.208.000.	000. The Prime Minister was blasting our trade and what was the result? A hole of $527,000,000 in that year. Had he any reason to say, "We have succeeded where others have failed"?
Our total trade in that same year was $1,706,000,000, a decrease of $662,000,000. Did the Prime Minister have any reason to say, "We have succeeded where others have failed"?
One would have thought that that was enough of that experiment; when the Prime Minister saw that the country was on the verge of ruin he should have changed his ways and abandoned his insane policy of high tariffs. On July 8, 1931, at page 3554 of Hansard, the Prime Minister admitted that he had changed in his first year of office nearly one-half of the total number of tariff items in the schedules. What was the result in the second year? Again, according to the official figures of the Department of Trade and Commerce for the year ending March 31,
1932,	our trade with the United Kingdom was $280,000,000. There was some blasting again. The new decrease in one year was $88,000,000, and two years' blasting resulted in a decrease of S190,000,000.
With the United States our trade was $586,000,000. As a result of the blasting of 1932 our trade with the United States decreased by $347,000,000, and in the two years there was a decrease of $775,000,000. Was it not a fine blast, Mr. Speaker?
Our trade with the British Empire for the year ending March 31, 1932, was $366,000,000,

showing a further decrease of $131,000,000, and a decrease in two years, after two formidable blasts, of $265,000,000. Had the Prime Minister any reason to say to this house that he had succeeded where others had failed? These figures are depressing, but in answer to the bombastic statements that we hear from the other side it is good to come down to plain facts, and my speech is very matter of fact as you must realize, Mr. Speaker.
With foreign countries our trade for the year ending March 31, 1932, was $788,000,000, a decrease in one year of $420,000,000, and in the two years there was a decrease of $948,000,000. Some blast!
Our total trade in that same year ending March 31, 1932, showed a new decrease of . $551,000,000. Our total trade for the year ending March 31, 1930, was $2,368,000,000, and for the year ending March 31, 1932, $1,154,000,000, a decrease in two years, after two successive blasts, of about $1,213,685,000. What a great chasm! How shall it be filled? By probabilities, possibilities and potentialities. That is all the government has to offer now.
But the same thing continues. According to a statement of the Department of National Revenue our imports for the month of September, 1931, were $45,000,000, and for the same month in 1932, $34,000,000. On the other hand, our exports for the same month in 1931 were $48,000,000, and for the same month in 1932, $42,000,000. After the last conference there was also a drop in our trade last month as compared with the previous year. I do not blame the members of the government so much as the Prime Minister himself for that. I regret to have to do it, but I feel it is my duty. The high tariff brought about by the Imperial economic conference reminds me of a client who came late one day to my office and said, "I do not feel well." I said: W'hait is the matter with you? He said, "I left home this afternoon quite late before taking my dinner, and on the train I bought a banana from the news agent. After I had eaten it I found it was rdtten." After having swallowed the agreements of the Imperial conference, if we may judge by his speech of last night, the Prime Minister must have the same feeling.
I wish to tell hon. members that we on this side of the house are willing to cooperate with the government, provided we are not addressed as schoolboys. Not one of us is a schoolboy; we are grown men and want to be treated as such by the Prime Minister. We want to be treated by him as well as

The Address-Mr. Pouliot
we are treated by his colleagues in the cabinet; they set a good example for him. If I were-thank God I am not-if I were on the other side of the house I would have spoken the same in caucus-

speechtext:
Oh, yes. I would have
spoken the same way in caucus as I have spoken this afternoon. I cannot understand how hon. members opposite can accept dictation from any one. When they are told to do this and that, they are just as quiet as schoolboys, and when the prophet opens his mouth they kneel down in deep respect. If I were on the other side of the house I could not live for one second; I should die of asphyxiation. Over here we breathe the free air of liberty; one is free to say that which he thinks proper. Hon. members are entirely free, and I am sure hon. members opposite envy us the happy position of being able to say what we think, and envy our earnest and sincere views, which are our own.
One word in conclusion, and it is this: I understand that because of the Prime Minister's stubbornness in keeping tariffs at such a high altitude the trade of Canada has been ruined. No hon. member opposite has courage enough to tell him that; they prefer to cheer and applaud him; they choose to encourage him in his bad ways, and in the wrong way. As members of the opposition it is our duty to tell him that which his supporters are too shy to place before him. We have to bring him down to realities, and to show him the deep chasm he has made by his blasting. When he said during the last election, he was to blast our way into the markets of the world, he was stating pure humbug. Although he did not give a definition of humbug, he himself gave a very good description of it. Our trade was to improve, conditions were to be much better for employers and employees in Canada. But we have only disaster and ruin, and possibly we are on the eve of a revolution. I hope God will never permit a revolution in Canada, but we do know that we heard last week of very unfortuante conditions. A spark may light a big fire. Then, the sad details outlined this afternoon by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) would indicate that that sentiment is growing in Canada. It is no time to fool the people; one must go to them and reason with them. One must not sit on a high tower, but must listen to the people and see what can be done for them. This is not the time to work so hard; hon. members in the government should learn that this is the
time to think. Let them think; let them stop working and begin thinking. I place on record those Latin words which I hope they have not forgotten: Desolatione desolata est terra, quia nullus est qui recogitet in suo corde. "The land is desolate to desolation because there is no one who thinks from the bottom of his heart." Let them think about the miseries of the people, about the coming winter. Let them think about their disastrous experiments in tariff legislation which have proved to be one of the greatest mistakes made in Canada. Let the government understand that railway employees are out of work because there is no traffic, and that there is no traffic because there is no trade. Let them cease to be so stubborn so that they may do something to help the men in industry.
Yesterday an apotheosis was outlined to the Liberal party, and when I make that statement of course I am referring to the speech by the Prime Minister. During the course of his remarks he mentioned occasionally the name of one of his predecessors, a leader of the Conservative party-Sir Charles Tupper. But when he wanted to shield himself, when he wanted to excuse himself for all the wrongs brought about by his nefarious policy of high tariffs, he invoked the memory of our own leader of other days, Sir Wilfrid Laurier. He mentioned that name not only once, but twice, three times, four times, ten times, twenty times, thirty times, and asked as many times that that great man should come to his rescue. Every time he uttered the name of that great leader of the Liberal party it was cheered to the echo by his own supporters in the Tory party. Sir, when Sir Wilfrid Laurier was in politics you were a young man; so was I, but I had great respect and affection for him. I knew him well enough to admire and not to forget him. We attend in this house at the cost of some sacrifice; we come here to do our duty, but there is a light showing us the way to come: the principles laid down by Sir Wilfrid Laurier. And when we see the leader of the Conservative party excusing himself, not by giving facts but by giving lectures, not by informing the people about the real situation but by promising possibilities, probabilities and potentialities, we say our duty is to fight his policy to the last ditch. In doing so we will live in accordance with the traditions of our own illustrious leader, Laurier.

iMr. YOUNG: One Statement he made attracted my attention. He said that if there was sufficient money in the hands of the people to buy production there could be no want, there could be no distress. I think we can all agree with that. How much money will be required in the hands of the people to buy production? Whatever money represents the amount of production you wish to buy. If you have a dollar in your possession it will buy one dollar's worth of production. If you tear that dollar in two and call each half one dollar the two halves will buy one dollar's worth of production. And by no trickery can you persuade people to give you two dollar's worth of production for the two half dollars which you call a dollar each.
If I understand aright, the arguments advanced by my hon. friends in the corner who believe in inflation are these: They do not pretend for a moment that anything we could do in the way of inflating our currency would have the effect of increasing world prices. No; they admit frankly that our wheat, lumber, pulpwood, newsprint, asbestos, copper, all the things we have to sell, would still ibe sold on the world market at world prices measured in terms of gold. For whatever we do with the gold standard, values will still be measured in gold throughout the world; whether we stay on it or not, whether other countries are on or off the gold standard, the world will still continue to measure values in gold. When Great Britain went off the gold standard, and said, we will no longer sell gold at so man}' grains to the pound, the

world said: Your pound is no longer worth $4.86 in gold; we will give you for your pound just what it is worth in gold. When Canada went off the gold standard and said: We will no longer give 25.8 grains of 90 per cent fine gold in exchange for the dollar, the world said: We will give you for your dollar just what it is worth in gold. So values will still be measured in gold.
So my friends admit that nothing we can do in the way of inflating our currency would affect world prices. But they say that after we have sold our wheat in the world market and received gold or its equivalent in exchange, if we inflate our currency we can turn that gold into more Canadian dollars than we do at present, and with these more Canadian dollars, even though they are not worth as much in gold, we shall be able to do more business in Canada. In support of that they quote wheat prices in Australia as against wheat prices in Canada. The freight rate on wheat, found in the same paper, September 28, from Melbourne to Liverpool, was 25s. per long ton, Australian funds. Figured in Canadian funds that is ten cents a bushel. The freight on wheat from Fort William to Liverpool, on the same date was 6-J cents to Montreal and 6 cents more to Liverpool, 12| cents a bushel. cents; it follows then that the price of wheat in Australia cn that day should have been 2J cents a bushel more than it was in Fort William. What was the price? Spot wheat, No. 1 northern, at Fort William, September 28, was 50 cents. The same spot wheat, Wil-liamstown basis, on the same date was 3s. 3|d. Australian funds, which translated into Canadian money is 50 cents a bushel. We were getting identically the same price, but we were paying 2J cents more freight than they were. Why did the Australian not get that extra 2} cents for his wheat? What became of it? One of two things: either he was selling wheat cheaper than we were in the Liverpool market, or those who were engaged in the export business in Australia were demanding a larger profit on their transactions because they were dealing in a fluctuating currency, which made an extra risk. They not only ran the risk of fluctuation in the price of the wheat but also the risk of fluctuation in the price of the money they were handling, and to cover that risk they insisted on a larger profit. In any event the Australian farmer was receiving, measured in terms of gold, or of Canadian currency, 2\ cents a bushel less than we were.
But my hon. friends say they are willing to lose that, because they say the 77 cents depreciated currency that the Australian farmer appears to receive-in reality it is only 50 cents-would enable him to pay more debts and to carry on to better advantage than the fifty cents which we receive. Let us examine that statement for a minute. The Australian dollar is down to approximately 50 cents, about half its value, Now, if the value of the dollar be cut in half, one would naturally suppose that prices would double. The Australian dollar being cut in half, the farmer in Australia should have received a dollar in Australian funds for his wheat where we were getting fifty cents. But he got only 77 cents.
In September, 1931, Great Britain went off the gold standard. Since then the price level in Great Britain has declined 2-7 per cent. My hon. friends say that if we go off the gold standard, depreciate our currency, prices will rise. But Great Britain's currency today is down about 30 per cent, yet the price level there has actually declined 2 per cent. There is an explanation for that. The United States stayed on the gold standard. Since Great Britain went off the gold standard, prices in the United States, that is gold prices, have declined; commodity prices in a country that is still on the gold standard have declined 14-4 per cent. The difference between 14-4 and 2-7 represents the effect of the depreciation of the pound on commodity prices in Great
Britain. I think I have Sir Josiah Stamp as my authority on that. That is, prices in terms of gold declined 14-4 per cent, but in a country that had gone off the gold standard prices declined only 2-7 per cent. Then we can say the depreciation in the pound was responsible for holding prices up, equal to the difference, between 14-4 and 2-7, or 11'7 per cent. The pound is down about 25 per cent, so in other words, the effect on price levels is just about half the amount of the inflation. Australia inflated her money to half its value and prices advanced to only about half that extent. Great Britain's currency has been inflated until it is worth about only 75 per cent of its former value, but prices have risen only 11-7 per cent. So I think we can safely say that to whatever extent we inflate our currency, prices will rise only to about half that extent.
My hon. friends propose that we tie our dollar to the pound sterling, which today is quoted at about $3.60 in Canadian funds. That would bring our dollar down to about 75 cents, so that where we now get $3 for a given product we would get four of the inflated dollars. The value would be the same, but we would get four of those dollars, and my friends in the corner say that with those four inflated dollars we will be able to pay more debts than we can pay with the three uninflated dollars. That is true, if the dollars would be used for that purpose, but today the price of wheat in western Canada is approximately 25 cents a bushel. We are going to inflate our currency until the dollar is worth about 75 cents. The British pound sterling is down 30 per cent below our currency. If we inflate by an additional 30 per cent we can expect an advance in the price level of about 15 per cent. Add 15 per cent to 25 cents a bushel and you get a probable increase in the price of wheat of about 4 cents a bushel, in this depreciated currency. The price today is 25 cents, so the farmer would get about 29 or 30 cents in the depreciated money, and I want to ask how many debts he would be able to pay with wheat at 30 cents a bushel.

I like to anchor to something firm and solid. Fifteen months ago the pound sterling was worth S4.86J. Great Britain went off the gold standard and immediately the pound dropped to S3.30. Later it rose to $4.20, but now it is back to $3.30. Is that a very good anchorage? We would foe anchoring to a floating cloud. Let me ask this

question: What causes the pound to rise and fall? What causes our dollar to rise and fall in the markets of the world? Why do these exchanges fluctuate? It is the supply and demand of dollars on the market that determines the value of our currency; it is the supply and demand of British pounds that determines the value of the pound. When you sell goods to Great Britain you get paid for them in Canadian money, but the buyer pays for them in British money. When he sells goods to us he gets paid in his own money, but we pay for those goods in our money. How is that arranged? When he buys Canadian goods he takes his British pounds to the market, sells them and buys Canadian dollars. When we want to buy goods in Great Britain, in order to pay him in his own currency we take our dollars to the market, sell them and buy British pounds. The more Canadian dollars there are for sale in the market and the less demand there is for them, the lower they go. Similarly, the more British pounds there are for sale in the market and the less demand there is for them, the lower they go.
So it is apparent that the value of the pound is determined by the trade situation in Great Britain, by her trade balance, if you like. The value of our dollar is determined by the trade balance of Canada, and when we undertake to tie our dollar to the British pound and, as my friend suggested the other night, pass an act providing that we will redeem the pound at par in our own currency, what are we doing? We are simply backing Britain's notes as far as she likes to issue them, and she is doing the same for us. Today the British pound is lower than it has been for some little time, and why? Because at this season of the year Great Britain is buying heavily of raw cotton. She is selling pounds in order to buy American dollars with which to pay for that cotton. We are not buying cotton today; we are selling wheat. Our sales are greater than our purchases at this time, so our dollar has gone up.
What could Great Britain do if we agreed to redeem her pound at par? She could pay for her cotton in this way: She could say: "We will not sell our pound in the United States to buy American dollars; we will pay for that cotton with Canadian dollars, because Canada will give us $4.86 for our pound." What would be the result? It would be that we, the Canadian people, would be taxing ourselves in order to buy Great Britain's raw cotton for her. That would be the inevitable result if we tied our dollar to the pound sterling.

My hon. friends seem to think that by increasing the volume of money in circulation the amount of business would be increased. I have before me a statement of the amount of money in the banks in July, 1930, and in September of this year. In a parallel column appears the debits against bank accounts. If you have ten dollars in your pocket or in your til! and you do one hundred dollars worth of business in a given time, you have turned your money over ten times; your money velocity is ten. Everybody knows that money turns over and over, and the number of times it turns over is the rate of the velocity of your money. The bank deposits in July, 1930, amounted to $2,034,000,000, the turnover or the debits against bank accounts amounted to $3,093,000,000; the velocity was 152 per cent, that is, the money was turning over one and one-half times in the month or at the rate of eighteen times in the year. In September of this year the bank deposits amounted to $1,841,000,000 and ths debits against bank accounts amounted to $2,097,000,000. The velocity was 113-9 per cent for the month, or thirteen and two-thirds times for the year. In July, 1930, we were turning our money over at the rate of eighteen times per year, today we are turning it over only at the rate of a little over thirteen times. If we go back to January, 1929, we will find that we were turning over our money at the rate of twenty-one times per year. If you increase the volume of your money without increasing the goods that are moving, what is going to happen? You will decrease the velocity. If the goods are there to be moved and nothing stops them from being moved, there is plenty of money with which to move them. Why? Because money today is travelling so slowly and when the demand for goods arises the velocity of money will increase. We do not need to do anything in connection with the money in circulation in order to increase business.

I know of no subject on which it is harder to keep one's mind clear than the currency question. A wise man once said to his son: "'Son, if you want to go crazy, study currency questions." But in order that we may not become too much confused in the matter, there are a few truths that we should keep in mind. The first is this, that when a man goes into the market to sell the products of his labour and takes money in exchange, he is entitled to receive money that represents the product of somebody else's labour. I think that even my hon. friends in the corner to my left will agree that. If that money does not represent somebody else's labour, you have no right to ask a man to sell his labour for worthless paper.
The question is how to find the best measure of the value of labour. You cannot say that one hour of your labour is worth cne hour of mine, because you might be a better workman, more skilful and you might apply yourself more closely than I. How are 3rou going to find an accurate measure of labour? Different ways have been suggested, but the way that has generally been accepted is this: men say: We will find some commodity that requires a constant amount of labour for its production. No such commodity exists, but the nearest we can come to it is gold. Gold represents labour and the value of the gold, that is not in terms of grains and so on, but the purchasing power of gold on the world market, depends upon the amount cf labour required to replace that gold. That can be easily demonstrated. If you were to go out and discover a mountain of gold, so plentiful and so easily mined that you could shovel it up like sand, gold would be of no value at all. Why? Because very little labour would be required in producing it. It is because there is so much labour required to produce a given quantity of gold that it becomes very valuable. It has been found that no other known commodity varies less than gold in respect of the amount of labour required to produce it. So men say: Let us take that as a measure of value for labour. I do not claim for a minute that it is a perfect measure. Certainly it is not. Time was when gold was produced at les3 cost than now; time was, probably, when it was produced at greater labour cost than now, but it is the best measure we have found so far. If my hon. friends can suggest any more accurate measurement of the value of labour 53719-55
than the amount of gold that can be produced in a given time, then I am willing to consider their proposition.
What do they offer us? What is the basis they offer for currency? They say they will have an intelligent inflation with a definite basis. What is the basis? Let us look at the subamendment cf the hon. member for Macleod, which reads:
And that the issue of this currency and credit should be based upon the natural wealth and productive capacity of this country, not, as at the present time, upon one single commodity, gold, and that its volume should be determined by the goods and services to be deaitli with, and the legitimate requirements of the people.
They are going to base our currency on our natural resources and our productive capacity. We have forests of timber and mines of ore; we have fields where we can grow wheat and lakes and streams where we can catch fish, and on these things they are going to base our currency. When the farmer comes into the market with his wheat and wants to sell it, what are they going to give him for it? A dollar that represents an interest in an untouched forest or an unopened mine. With this money they are going to purchase the products of the farm, the forest, the lake and the mine. I ask the house this: What wilt our producers of wealth say, what will the world say, when we offer them this dollar in exchange for goods? They will say "There is no market for trees standing in the forest or fish swimming in the sea or ore lying in the mine. This dollar of yours which represents these things cannot be exchanged for consumable goods; we cannot give you anything for it." Our dollar would be worthless. Will the world take more of our wheat if you change our currency in that way ? Will it take any more of our lumber or asbestos or copper? Nothing you can do with our currency can open the world's markets. As I said before, the trouble is not with the amount of currency we have, but with the fact that the goods are not moving. Create the condition where the goods will move and currency will take care of itself.

maintopic: QUESTIONS
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
May I assure you, Mr. Speaker, at the very outset that it is not my intention to delay the house at this juncture with any lengthy oration or prolonged or extended remarks. It is my purpose chiefly to make a somewhat brief statement dealing in the main with one phase of the amendment now before us and to indicate as clearly and as definitely as possible my own attitude and that of those for whom I speak in respect to this amendment. Before doing so, however, may I offer a few very brief observations of a more general character which may serve as a background for the statement which I have in mind?
We meet here today under conditions and amidst circumstances that are a challenge to every member of this house, a challenge alike to our intelligence, our sincerity and our courage. We are faced by difficulties so great and by responsibilities so tremendous as to dwarf into paltry insignificance every consideration of political partisanship and political expediency, preconceived opinion and petty personal prejudice. We stand, parliament and the administration and the various institutions of which they form a part, before the bar of an aroused public opinion, and we shall be judged and shall stand or fall as we meet these difficulties and solve these problems in the interests of those whom we represent, for whom we are the trustees, and who are looking to us to-day in anxious and sometimes almost despairing expectation for guidance and leadership, and for action, prompt, definite and courageous.
Nor, Mr. Speaker, are these difficulties wholly insuperable or these problems wholly insoluble, although some, not all, are international in character and susceptible only to international cooperation and international action.
We in common with other nations are staggering beneath a load of international liabilities. We are surrounded by world tariffs impregnable to our assaults. Our foreign trade is hampered, our exports are restricted by world barriers, but many of these problems, and some of the first magnitude, are mainly, if not wholly, domestic in their character and are amenable to our parliamentary action. It is true that our foreign and export trade is hampered and frustrated by world restrictions, but it is equally true that we have within the confines of our own country, to say nothing of the empire, natural wealth and productive capacity sufficisat to provide within Canada and for all our people a stands ard of living higher and more secure than anything we have yet enjoyed.
53719-5SJ
It has been stated very often, and reiterated with such frequency as to have become almost axiomatic and accepted by many as a fact, that this country, and particularly western Canada, has been built and developed on export trade, that it is essential to our national existence, and that without it we must perish; and yet, Mr. Speaker, if you analyze that statement and subject it to close and logical scrutiny, I think you will agree with me that that is so farcical, so utterly false, as to be a fantastic absurdity. It is true, and we will admit it at once, that export trade is a very vital part of our present economic system, and that its cessation would necessitate drastic and fundamental changes in our entire outlook and in our methods of production and marketing. But to say that, because we grow more food, for example, in this country than may be consumed by our entire population, and are unable to dispose of the surplus to other lands for this reason, and as an inevitable consequence one-third of our people must suffer hardships and one-fifth must face starvation, is a positive absurdity, nothing more or less. I spoke of a challenge to our intelligence, and there is one-starvation in the midst of plenty. We know this phrase has been used so often as to become, to many, perfectly meaningless; it has come to be associated in many minds with	tub thumping and soap	box	oratory.Yet, if we analyze that phrase and look it straight in the face it becomes no mere phrase, but takes the form of a terrible and grotesque reality; it becomes a monumental and damning indictment upon our modern civilization. Starvation in the midst of plenty-a domestic problem, surely, and one within the competence of our own parliament. And while our	hungry	cry	for	bread,	our	farmerswho	produce	it	are	groaning	beneath theweight of impossible liabilities, of high interest rates and of price levels for all their products far below the cost of production. Can not this	problem	lbe	met	and solved,	or must
parliament and its leaders prove themselves as void and bankrupt of statesmanship and genius as our farmers of money?
It is not that we are asked to perform the impossible. Parliament is not asked to meet and to overcome the dire consequences of some destructive cataclysm of nature; we are not asked to produce wealth from barren ground. That wealth has been produced, and by those people whom we now represent. Our warehouses are filled with goods to meet our needs, ample for our requirements. What is lacking, and apparently all that is required, is money-money for our use, to facilitate our
The Address-Mr. Speakman

business, to permit the passage of these goods from him who has to him who needs, who in turn may possess that which the first man would secure. It would seem, however, that our financial structure has failed us and our money machine no longer functions. Yet in that condition, one obvious to all, we are assured through the lips of His Excellency the Governor General that the financial integrity of this nation has been maintained and is secure.
But what is the nation? Is it to be found in our wide acres, our spreading forests and our mines? Is that the nation; is it to be found in our tall buildings, our vaulted banks? Or, are these few men who control, or who have failed to control, that money machine wdiich no longer serves us-are these the nation? Rather, Mr. Speaker, the nations is our ten millions of people found everywhere in Canada, our farmers toiling in their fields-* courageous still, in near despair-our clerks, our business and professional men, striving against impossible odds to maintain their businesses, preserve their livelihoods and keep up appearances; our miners, our fishermen, our factory hands. These are the nation, the toiling multitudes within our borders who by brawn or brain produce our wealth and provide the foundation of ail our credit and all this nation's finance. They are the nation. Yes, Mr. Speaker, and even that vast army of unemployed who are crowding our cities, wandering along our highways, burrowing in our dump heaps, cursing, some of them, both God and man, and believing in neither, they too are the nation, and they look to us for action-not for words, for action.
Meanwhile a majority in this parliament, and its leaders, put their trust in ancient precepts, hold fast to old notions and strive to meet modern problems with ancient and timeworn methods. They prate of sound money as of a God, and dismiss any suggestion not hoary with age with the contemptuous appellation of a "nostrum" or a "quack remedy." Among the greatest of the powers which we hold with which to meet the situation is the control, vested in this parliament, of currency, credit and finance. As has (been stated, it is true we have farmed this out, this power and this responsibility and given it to private hands. Although we .may have done that we cannot divest ourselves of either power or responsibility, and in the subamendment there was a call upon the administration to resume one and to exercise the other to meet the nation's need and the people's good.
In the moving of the amendment now before us we saw a ray of hope, a hope that the

leader of the opposition and the great party which gave it sanction had seen the light and recognized the need. We recognized also that this conversion, if real, was of very recent date. We knew that within the last few months the leader of the opposition had vied with and even excelled the Prime Minister in reviling and condemning our suggestions. Although we recognized that the amendment as it stood was empty, meaningless and void, composed wholly of regrets, wholly negative and nothing positive, we saw that it might be made to mean something. We did not feel we should disturb one line of it, but left it as it stood, word for word, and endeavoured merely to add something to it which would make it positive, which would put meaning into it, and which, if accepted, would in its last phrase promise definite action.
Since the two amendments were moved, however, the situation has changed somewhat. I had in mind to judge of the sincerity of the Liberal party by their attitude towards the subamendment, but now I think of something that happened a day or two ago. I recall that the leader of the opposition and almost every member of his party then voted for parts of the suggestion we brought forward in an amendment we then moved, and which had for its purpose the bringing of our dollar to a parity with the English pound. To that degree at least they put sincerity and meaning into their protestations as to the necessity for dealing with the monetary system. Because they have promised action when the time may come, because they put something positive in their promise through their action and vote at that time, because their regrets carry with them the promise of something positive and some future action, and because of the saving remnant in the Liberal party who see as we see, who understand that we cannot conquer present difficulties, that we cannot conquer vast and complex problems with old-time worn out methods-because of all those things, for those who think as I do and for myself may I say that we shall give them the benefit of the doubt and shall support their amendment.

Practically all barbed wire recently used in Alberta and western Saskatchewan comes from Holland manufacturer whom we represent and is sold by prairie wholesalers very cheap whereby farmers greatly benefit. I cannot at all agree with the statement that Ottawa admits that there is no dumping of barbed wire. On the contrary, the Department of National Revenue is satisfied that there is dumping by a German

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT

speechtext: The right hon. leader of the opposition on Friday last, at page 848 of Hansard, asked me a question, and in reply I desire to say, first, not having the context before me, I do not think it is desirable to make any answer to the question. In the second place, it would be improper for me to do so inasmuch as it affects the other dominions as well as this, and any construction I might place on any word might be at variance with that which might be placed upon it by the governments of the other dominions. I think that in the progress of the recent discussion it was made abundantly clear what was the position of this country and what our legal rights are, and so far as I have been able to see there has not been anything said by the government in Great Britain which, taken with its context, means other than what has been said in this house by the government.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT
subtopic: POWER OF PARLIAMENT IN CANADA OR GREAT BRITAIN TO ALTER OR ABROGATE
speechtext: Apart altogether from the context, may I ask the Prime Minister this question? If a statement were made in the British house to the effect that the rates of duty substituted by the Anglo-Canadian pact for existing Canadian duties could not be altered within the next five years except to a limited degree specified in the agreement, or if that statement were made in this house or anywhere else, would it be correct?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT
subtopic: POWER OF PARLIAMENT IN CANADA OR GREAT BRITAIN TO ALTER OR ABROGATE
speechtext:
The statement that we
had entered into a contract for a period of five years within the terms of the contract would be correct. We have made a contract for five years, and the terms are set forth in the agreement, and when they have been ratified they are binding upon this country.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT
subtopic: POWER OF PARLIAMENT IN CANADA OR GREAT BRITAIN TO ALTER OR ABROGATE
speechtext:
I am afraid
my right hon. friend is evading the question.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT
subtopic: POWER OF PARLIAMENT IN CANADA OR GREAT BRITAIN TO ALTER OR ABROGATE
speechtext:
No. I do not intend to
answer it.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT
subtopic: POWER OF PARLIAMENT IN CANADA OR GREAT BRITAIN TO ALTER OR ABROGATE
speechtext: May I ask my right hon. friend specifically whether this parliament has not the right to alter, within the next five years, any duties that may happen to be included in the agreement?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT
subtopic: POWER OF PARLIAMENT IN CANADA OR GREAT BRITAIN TO ALTER OR ABROGATE
speechtext:
I made it perfectly clear
the other day, and I desire to repeat, lest there be any misunderstanding, that the power of this parliament is unlimited. Its honour is bound. Whether the right hon. gentleman would carry into effect the threat he made the other day, that if he was in power he would change these agreements, is not for me to say, but so far as we can in honour we have bound this parliament for a term of years and on the terms mentioned.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT
subtopic: POWER OF PARLIAMENT IN CANADA OR GREAT BRITAIN TO ALTER OR ABROGATE
speechtext: I want to take exception to my right hon. friend's statement that I have made any threat. I have made no threat of any kind. I want to make it clear, however, that the Liberal party will not regard itself as in honour bound to maintain any policies of hon. gentlemen opposite which are diametrically opposed to those of the party.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: REMEMBRANCE DAY ADJOURNMENT-PROCEDURE RESPECTING TRADE AGREEMENTS
speechtext: I believe business would be expedited if the house as soon as possible were to go into committee of ways and means to consider the proposed changes in the tariff which have been placed before the house.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: REMEMBRANCE DAY ADJOURNMENT-PROCEDURE RESPECTING TRADE AGREEMENTS
speechtext: I propose to proceed first with the first reading of the bill based upon the resolution passed the other evening respecting a certain trade agreement between His Majesty's government in Canada and His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom, and probably the second reading as well. I can give the reasons now or later, just as the hon. gentleman prefers.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: REMEMBRANCE DAY ADJOURNMENT-PROCEDURE RESPECTING TRADE AGREEMENTS
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman might give them now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: REMEMBRANCE DAY ADJOURNMENT-PROCEDURE RESPECTING TRADE AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
The agreement entered
into at Ottawa between the representatives of the United Kingdom and the representatives of the government of Canada sets forth in schedule E certain changes which are to be made in our tariff. The changes were not set out in detail, but simply with relation to the items that would be affected by them. Hence it was that when the Australian Trade Agreement Act was introduced on June 23, 1925, it was then read the first and second times, considered in committee, reported without amendment, read a third time and passed- all on the same day; no reference, of course, being made to the ways and means committee.
The French Convention Act of 1923 dealt with a very large number of items, but no more in point of fact than does the trade agreement here, if you total the items of both the French and the Canadian tariffs. That bill was introduced on February 20, 1923, and was then read a first time. It was read a second time on April 26, 1923, and then referred to the committee of the whole, from which it was reported without amendment on April 30. It was read a third time on May 1, 1923, and passed, and there was no reference to the committee of ways and means. The trade Convention Act between Canada and Finland was introduced upon a resolution and read a first time on May 14, 1925. It was read a second time, referred to the committee of the whole and reported without amendment on May 18,

1925. It was read a third time on May 19. 1925.	'
The Italian Convention Act was introduced on May 2, 1923, was then read a first and second time, referred to the committee of the whole, reported without amendment, and ordered for third reading at the next sitting of the house. It was read a third time on May 14, 1923, without reference to the committee of ways and means.
Had it not been for the fact that it was imperative that the items mentioned in schedule E should be put in form agreeable to the nomenclature in our tariffs and that some items which were rather cumbersome should be split into several items, it would not have been essential to refer the matter to the committee of ways and means; but in view of that fact, and the further fact that these tariffs are substituted for British preferential tariffs in the tariff schedules of the country, it was thought desirable to refer the matter to the committee of ways and means. The agreement ratifies and confirms the agreement as entered into, and the schedules referred to the ways and means committee are schedules that give effect in detail to the provisions of schedule E. Under those circumstances we propose to proceed with the ratification of the agreement by enacting a statute in form similar to that which was used in the ratification of the agreement with Australia in 1923 and of the agreements with Italy, France and Finland, and then proceed further with the changes to the tariff legislation that are brought about by reason of the ratification of the agreement.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: REMEMBRANCE DAY ADJOURNMENT-PROCEDURE RESPECTING TRADE AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
I understand
from what my right hon. friend says that he does not propose to allow us to discuss the proposed tariff changes until we have approved the agreement. That is what it comes to, is it not?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: REMEMBRANCE DAY ADJOURNMENT-PROCEDURE RESPECTING TRADE AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
It is proposed to proceed as was done by my right hon. friend when he was on the treasury benches, namely, ratify the agreement by the vote of this parliament, based upon the resolution, and then proceed with the tariff changes as I indicated for the reasons I have given. I could amplify them, but they must be apparent to every member.
I would hardly think that the right hon. gentleman seriously meant that there would be any effort on the part of the government to preclude discussion. After having listened to or having read, at least, what has transpired for three weeks, I do not think it can be said that there has been any disposition on the part of the government to limit discussion writh respect to anything.

Income War Tax Act

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: REMEMBRANCE DAY ADJOURNMENT-PROCEDURE RESPECTING TRADE AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
I do not wish
to appear to be debating any subject with my right hon. friend, but he asked at the outset as to what would facilitate the business of the house. I understand that these several measures contemplate changes in the tariff, that they are inter-related, also that question will arise as to the significance of the changes on each of the separate measures.
I believe we would finish more quickly if we discussed the tariff changes in the first instance, so that we may have a better understanding as to what is really involved by each and all of the several agreements. There would be very little time taken up in debating the different measures if we once understood what the tariff changes involved amount to. I do submit, however, that if we are asked by approval of the agreements in advance to make tariff changes without knowing their significance we are being asked to take an almost impossible position, and one which I am afraid will prolong discussion very much.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: REMEMBRANCE DAY ADJOURNMENT-PROCEDURE RESPECTING TRADE AGREEMENTS
speechtext: The house is being asked to do exactly what the right hon. gentleman did when he was leader. There is this exception, however, that we are affording the house an opportunity for detailed discussion of every item in the ways and means committee, so far as the United Kingdom tariff is concerned-an opportunity which was not afforded heretofore. I think the right hon. gentleman will agree that if he were in my place he would certainly desire that the legislation which gives the warrant for the ways and means committee to sit should be enacted, so far as the house is concerned, to the point where it is ready for third reading before the discussion in ways and means committee takes place. It must be apparent to every hon. member that, except by consent of the United Kingdom government, we cannot change, modify or amend the agreement as it stands. There are one or two items in connection with which there are slight changes which I propose to make known to the house on the first reading of the bill.

maintopic: INCOME WAR TAX ACT

speechtext:
Hon. E. N. RHODES (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into oommittee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to amend the Income War Tax Act and to provide,-
1.	That ministers, commissioners, officers, servants and employees of the government resident outside of Canada be made liable for income tax.
2.	That when the assets or shares of a company, having on hand undistributed income at
the end of 1929, are sold directly or through an intermediary to a company, which company issues shares, bonds, notes or other like documents as fully paid up by capitalizing the said undistributed income, then on the redemption of such documents the company redeeming shall pay a tax of four per centum on the amount of such document redeemed.
3.	That the time of filing information returns be advanced from March 31st to the last day of February in each year.
4.	That the provisions of the said act with respect to personal corporation be amended to make them more certain in their application.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: INCOME WAR TAX ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
the resolution is fairly clear with the exception of paragraphs 2 and 4. Possibly the minister would give some explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Would it not be better

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
