speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the first
clause in the resolution is necessitated by the fact that while it has hitherto been the intention that the salaries of ministers, as such, should not be subject to income tax, the position has heretofore been taken that ministers and others designated in this paragraph have not been residents of Canada, but of other countries. The result has been that they have escaped the payment of income tax upon their personal incomes apart from their salaries. The purpose of this amendment is to make it clear that their incomes shall be taxable, as if they were residents of Canada.

maintopic: INCOME WAR TAX ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, are these
employees of the government subject to the income taxes of the countries in which they reside? And, the further question: Are the public servants of other countries resident in Canada subject to Canadian income tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: INCOME WAR TAX ACT
speechtext: In most instances, Mr. Chairman, it has been a matter of mutual arrangement. We, in Canada, do not tax representatives of foreign countries upon their salaries.

maintopic: INCOME WAR TAX ACT
speechtext:
It would not be fair to tax
them twice.
Income War Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: INCOME WAR TAX ACT
speechtext:
No. With respect to the
second paragraph, probably I would do well to defer explanation until we have reached committee stage on the bill. I may say, however, that the necessity for this legislation arises through a series of technicalities, a court interpretation, and amendments to the Income War Tax Act. Perhaps I might say in connection with paragraph 2-and the same statement would apply to the whole bill-that the amendments are entirely in keeping with the original intention of the act, and tend simply to remove existing doubts.
The third paragraph is self-explanatory. Then, as to the fourth there is an endeavour to make clear the original intention of the act. The purpose of the clause is to make sure that incomes from personal corporations shall be fully taxed in Canada. It has transpired that such corporations have been set up outside of Canada, although managed within Canada. The result has been that in many instances we have not received income tax from those personal corporations. The act will provide, if the suggested amendment becomes law, that hereafter notwithstanding the fact that the personal corporation is outside of Canada, the individual in Canada shall be subject to the provisions of the Canadian income tax legislation.

maintopic: INCOME WAR TAX ACT
speechtext: Is the minister making provision for the taxing of bearer bonds? I think I dealt with that matter last year when another resolution was before the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: INCOME WAR TAX ACT

The hon. member will see
that there is a resolution upon the order paper with respect to that very subject. I would not care to make an announcement now, but there will be an announcement before the session is concluded which I trust will be satisfactory.

In this section of the

I believe they are already subject to the income taxes obtaining in the countries in which they live. In that event they -would be paying an income tax not only to outside governments, but to the government in Canada. IV ill the tax they pay to foreign governments be subtracted from their salaries, and if so will they be required to pay Canadian income tax in accordance with
[Mr. Euler.l
their salaries, less the amount they pay in taxes to the countries in which they live, or, will they be taxed upon their whole salaries?

maintopic: INCOME WAR TAX ACT

Mr. Chairman, my hon.
friend from Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), I think did not hear the explanation I made a moment ago. It was to the effect that the act proposes that we shall tax the income of those individuals apart from their salaries, and that income apart from their salaries is not taxable in other countries.

maintopic: INCOME WAR TAX ACT

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES

speechtext:
Hon. II. II. STEVENS (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved the second reading of Bill No. 9, to amend the Canada Grain Act. (Domestic grain).
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. LaVergne in the chair.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: I would like to ask the minister what the charges are now and what they have been during the past two or three years. We all know that the farmer today is getting a very small price for his grain. It seems to me that under present conditions the charges for cleaning and inspection and weighing should be reduced in order that the load on the farmer may be lessened somewhat. Under present conditions the charges seem very unfair. Elevation, for example, used to cost 1 cent a bushel, now some of our country elevators are charging 2i cents. It is time these charges were brought down to where they were when the price of wheat was somewhat nearer what it is at the present time.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext:
Precisely what my hon.
friend desires is what this bill empowers the board of grain commissioners to do. Under the Canada Grain Act, once a year the board of grain commissioners meet and fix fees for the ensuing year. They hold hearings throughout the country, and anyone who has any grievance may come before the board and

Canada Grain Act
express his views. Advantage is sometimes taken of this opportunity. The practice hitherto has been to fix the rates at a time just prior to the movement of the new crop, usually during the month of August. This practice was followed this year; no protests were filed with the board, no complaints made with the exception of one individual complaint, as to the rates charged by the elevators. But the government, reviewing the situation, realized that owing to the fall in the value of grains, wheat particularly, the charges for storage entailed a somewhat heavy percentage of the value of the grain. The storage rate at present is 1/30 of a cent a day, one cent a month. 1 am not desirous today of stating dogmatically what the new rate will be, but we are providing in this bill power for the board of grain commissioners to vary the charge, the intention being that the charge will be reduced to a point considered reasonable in the light of all the facts now prevalent. I would say it will likely be a very substantial reduction in the storage charges.
The bill is a very simple one, I do not think there is any need to go into an exhaustive discussion about matters that might be relevant but not profitable to discuss now. That is the simple point in the bill, that section 134 should ibe amended to permit the board of grain commissioners, by regulation or by action of the board, to reduce rates between the times at present fixed by statute.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: Do you include inspection and weighing?

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: Inspection and weighing will also come under review if the bill passes. All charges.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: IC does not mention inspection and weighing.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: All charges. The word "handling" covers the whole business.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: Is not the minister putting in the hands of the grain commission complete authority and control over charges to be levied on grain?

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext:
No more than they have at present-let us be perfectly clear on that -except in one respect. Hitherto, under section 134, such action by the board could be taken only once a year, and the fees having been fixed the board could not make any change except subject to some other paragraphs in the act. The only object we have in view is this: During this time of stress the board is precluded from taking any action and we want to empower them to take action.
I may say there is a very general willingness and desire, lam informed today, on the part of the elevator companies to conform to any reasonable action of the board. In fact it is possible they may take action even before this bill is passed. I am certain that there is a willingness and desire to meet this situation and all who are interested in lessening the burden of costs upon this commodity will welcome this privilege being given to the board of grain commissioners at this time.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext:
I would like to make an observation. The minister speaks of this being a very simple change. It is, but in my opinion it is a very dangerous change. My reason for saying that is that while the power given the board may in this particular instance be for the most laudable of objects, it also makes it possible for the board to raise rates between seasons, after the whole question of rate charges has been argued out at the first sitting. This might not be nearly so laudable as the object which the minister presents at this time.
I think the minister might also explain to the house, in introducing this bill, just what reason there is for reducing storage charges at the present time; whether or not the government is supporting the idea of holding wheat, and whether the government has been supporting the wheat market by carrying big stocks of wheat in the hands of the pool. There is no doubt that the American farm loan board experienced a very serious loss by holding wheat. It is quite possible that the attempt to steady the wheat market may mean a very serious loss to the pool, and if storage charges are to be lowered to the point where they become infinitesimal they may be also wiped out by this change. On the other hand, at some future time when it \\ ould be to the interests of the elevator companies to raise charges, they could be raised.
I am going to say to my hon. friend the minister that I have not the slightest objection to giving the board power at present to lower rates or handling charges or anything else, but I do not want to subscribe to a bill which gives them the broad power to raise rates, it they see fit to do so, after the crop season is open and the farmers know what rates they expect to pay during the ensuing year. I think the minister is putting a lot of power into the hands of the board for what at the moment may seem desirable.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext:
This bill contains a provision with regard to the storage of wheat. We find that in the elevators we have wheat
Canada Grain Act

that has been stored for many years, and I have been told that the elevators will not be able to store the crop this year. Therefore I take the liberty of suggesting to the government that when navigation closes some ships should be chartered in order to provide sufficient storage this year. Then I should like to ask the minister what amounts have oeen guaranteed by the government to the pool for wheat purchases during the last two years.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext:
My hon. friend has raised a point in connection with the storage of wheat. I presume it is quite true that if we tried to put all the wheat in Canada into storage at the present time our facilities would be taxed beyond their capacity, but I believe there is reasonably ample storage. There will be no trouble in that connection, I am confident. With regard to the use of vessels for storage purposes, that has been the practice for as long as I can remember, at least for thirty years. When the freeze-up comes in the east vessels are used for winter storage; that is a very common trade practice. I may reassure my hon. friend; I do not anticipate any difficulty in handling the grain that may come forward. There always have been and always will be periods of congestion during the handling of our grain crop, but when pressure becomes too heavy at one point it usually finds an outlet elsewhere.
In connection with the last question of the hon. gentleman, Mr. Chairman, I think it would be inadvisable to wander very far afield in this discussion. When the grain estimates are up 1 will be happy indeed to go into all phases of the grain trade, but I am pressing this bill now, in this emergent session, because I consider the purpose for which the bill is introduced as an emergent demand. I ask the house to simply receive the bill in its very simple form and pass it or otherwise as the case may be.
I can assure my hon. friend from North Bruce (Mr. Malcolm) that I have no anxiety along the lines he has mentioned. We are not enlarging the powers of the board; we are merely saying that instead of those pow'ers being limited, as they are under this section, to one period of the year when the fees can be fixed, the board may exercise those same powers during other parts of the year if they find it necessary to do so. The Canada Grain Act is a well established act that has been administered by various commissions, very successfully and very satisfactorily, for many years. I do not think the powers given the board have been abused.

The commission exercises these powers under well established practices and rules, and I think a careful perusal of the act will show that at almost every point there are safeguards in regard to these matters. The board is not going to act recklessly under these enlarged powers, and I submit to the house that at this time it is highly desirable that the board should be released from this restriction in order that we may give some relief to the western farmer in connection with storage charges, in the movement of this crop which is being sold at such low commodity prices.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: I have every sympathy with the intention of this bill, but I should like to point out to the minister that the relief to the western farmer will be almost negligible. I have not the grain act before me, and I know the minister has a copy under his hand. I should like to ask the minister if, instead of leaving the board with an absolutely free hand in this connection, he might consider it desirable to include in this bill a limitation as to the maximum charge?

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: So far as I am concerned I am quite willing to limit this bill to reductions only.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: If the minister would change the wording to read "shall not be reduced during any crop year except by order of the board," I think he would cover the point. Then it could not be increased.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: I do not take objection on that score, but let us assume that next week the board passes an order reducing these charges. How many farmers in western Canada will profit by that action? Almost seventy-five per cent of the farmers have sold their wheat.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: No.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext:
I beg my hon. friend's pardon; I think if he will make a careful estimate he will find that I am correct. Therein lies the chief virtue of having the price fixed before the crop movement commences; the farmer then gets some benefit from the fixation of the handling charges. I can tell my hon. friend that he is not going to help the farmer very much by any reduction at the present time, or in the middle of any crop movement. By that time the farmer has disposed of his crop, and it is in the hands of the trade. That is one reason why I take exception to the bill. I do not object to the board having the right to increase or

Canada Grain Act
decrease the charges, but the old method of fixing charges prior to the movement of the crop certainly ensures to the farmer his share of any reduction that may be made.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: Could the minister tell us how much grain is in storage at the present time ?

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: I could not tell my hon. friend offhand, but I know there is a very considerable quantity. I must speak without any authority before me, but I would say there is probably 130,000,000 bushels in storage.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: Would the minister consider the suggested amendment?

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: Yes, but frankly I think it would be a little difficult to draft it in connection with this clause. If we take up an amendment of that kind I am afraid we will have to take up the act as it relates to the fixation of charges. I chose this method because it is simpler. I can assure the house that there is only one object in bringing forward this bill, and that is the object I have stated. My hon. friend from West Edmonton suggests that the farmers would receive no benefit this year. I am strongly advised that this is not so, because a very substantial portion of this year's crop has not yet reached the elevators. I think anyone from the west will agree with that statement, though certainly some of the crop has gone forward. I have been considering this question for only a short time, and I wished to act quickly in order to give at least the maximum benefit to the farmers this year.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: Could the minister tell us about what reduction he proposes in the storage rate?

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: I have no objection to saying what is my view; I would say %5 instead of %o. Of course that is in the hands of the board; I am not going to dictate to them, but since my hon. friend has asked me I will tell him frankly what is my view.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext:
What charge does the
minister propose to make with respect to inspection and weighing? Most of the farmers' grain at the present time has been inspected and weighed and paid for. The grain has passed into terminal or private elevators in the country, and most of it is in the hands of neither of these two; it is in the hands of the trade. This will not benefit the farmer. There is no doubt about that. With regard to grain that is going in, what reduction does the minister propose to make in connection with weighing and inspection, and so on all
the way through, so that some benefit may accrue to the farmer?

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext:
That question I am not
prepared to answer at the moment; it is a question that will have to be carefully considered by the board. The main point is the cost of storage. My hon. friend shakes his head. Well, I suggest that his statement that most of the grain is now in the hands of the dealers is not correct; it would be overstating it to say that half the crop is. I think figures could be produced to show that. But that is not worth haggling about. There is a substantial portion of the crop still in the hands of the original owners.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext:
My hon.
friend does not suggest that 50 per cent is in the hands of the farmers, either in storage or in granaries.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: I certainly do.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: I do not think I am very far out. I do not wish to bandy words with my hon. friends opposite with regard to this question. I am acting in good faith; I am not trying to put anything over.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext:
Nobody is
suggesting that.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext:
As regards the question
of inspection fees, weighing and handling charges and so forth, I am not prepared to give an expression of view today; I think it would be foolish for me to do so. It is a highly technical matter that requires a great deal of consideration. The board has the question under consideration at the moment, at my request, and will decide what, in their opinion, is the wisest course to follow in that respect. Under pressure I have given my views with regard to charges in storage, and I think they are reasonable in the light of the fall in commodity prices and the drop in the general cost of handling. I think we are justified in suggesting a figure of that kind, but it will be in the hands of the board to determine what ultimately shall be done.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: Has the request for this bill come from the trade or from the commission itself, or from the department?

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: It has come from myself, has been opposed by the trade, and latterly has support from the farmers.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext:
Then, in view of the
statement made by the minister, that it comes from him, I would point out that he has
sso
Canada Grain Act

included in the bill charges in connection with the cleaning, storage and handling of grain in any public terminal.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext:
He has it in the bill
and does not propose to discuss it. Why was it put in the bill? When the minister is sponsor and originator of it, surely he can give us the reasons.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: That is scarcely a proper question; at least it is not stated in a proper form.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: Why not?

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: I have not put it in the bill; it is in the act now. I do not wish to get irritated with my hon. friend, ibut, frankly, he is not fair. I did not put it in the bill, I repeat. The bill simply adds seven or eight words to a clause already in the act.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext:
Let us read it. The clause as it now stands reads:
Notwithstanding in this act, the tariff of charges made for cleaning, storage and handling of grain in any public or semi-public or terminal or eastern elevator shall not be subject to change during the crop year.
Two weeks ago I suggested to the board that a reduction in charges should be made, but they drew my attention to this provision and said they were sorry but they could not do anything. We studied the problem very carefully and it was suggested in this conference that the best way to deal with the matter was, instead of going into a revision of the sections of this bill with regard to inspection charges, that we should simply add these words to this clause, which would make it permissible for the board to deal with the matter. And now my hon. friend upbraids me because I have not come here-

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext:
I did not.
Mr. STEVEN'S: Yes, my hon. friend upbraids me because I have not come here prepared to discuss the technique, the fairness or otherwise, of handling charges and so forth. I have very fair views on these things, but I think it would be presumptuous of me to say to the house that handling charges should be this, that and the other, where we have our highly trained staff, an excellent commission to deal with the very subject. I repeat, this question will 'be in the hands of the board, in whom I have confidence, and I would remind my hon. friends opposite that the personnel of the board comprises gentlemen whom they themselves appointed.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: We are not questioning that.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: I have very great confidence in the chairman and in all the members of the board, and I am prepared to leave it to their judgment. As I have said, I have certain views on the question of storage, handling charges, weighing and so on, but these are matters upon which I prefer not to express my own opinion because my own opinion is not of sufficient authority, or ought not to be, to influence the house.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext:
If the grain trade are
opposing this legislation, one would naturally suppose that they do not own any of the wheat now held in storage. Can the minister give us an idea as to who does own it?

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext:
I can only say that my
hon. friend's guess is as good as mine. The grain in the storage, elevators is owned by the large grain companies such as Bungey. Dreyfus, Richardson and other companies, and the pools-three pools are operating now separately I think-own substantial quantities. There must be and always are substantial quantities of grain held in the various terminal elevators by individuals, farmers on a large scale and others who have merely carload lots, and also by small dealers. The grain is held now exactly as it has always been held. I can assure my hon. friend that there is nothing in the world behind this bill except the one thought in my own mind, which has been concerning me for several weeks, namely, the desire to lessen the burden of charge against the movement of grain, and I am hoping that the maximum result null go to the farmers. I am a little sorry, I confess frankly, that I had not the matter in my mind earlier. It had escaped my notice that when the board fixed the rate it was fixed for the whole season. That is a point that had not been in my mind. I may have been ?t fault; perhaps I should have been apprised of all the details. However, when I came to study the matter three weeks ago these difficulties presented themselves and this is the solution. I repeat, there is not a thing in my mind prompting this except the one desire to lessen the burden of charge on the movement of grain and, as I say, I trust that the maximum return will go to the owner of the grain, namely, the farmer.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext:
I am not
taking exception to the amendment on the ground that it gives power either to increase or to reduce rates. I well remember the discussion on this very section when the grain

Canada Grain Act
8S1
act was lip for revision. It was contended that it would be very much in the interests of the producer to have the rates fixed at the beginning of the season. My hon. friend states that at least 50 per cent of the crop is out of the hands of the producer.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext:
I did not say that. I
said I thought I was stating an excessive amount.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext:
May I say
to my hon. friend that even if you take into consideration the subscribers to the pool, who, of course, would benefit by this-that I am willing to admit-even allowing for those producers who are a very considerable number in the western provinces, I have not any doubt that more than 50 per cent of this year's crop is now out of the hands of the producers who will not benefit one iota by this provision.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext:
What about the other
50 per cent or even 35 or 40 per cent?

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext:
You can
take the other 50 per cent and divide it by two, and then you will have a generous division; that is to say, 25 per cent of it will be in the hands of the producers at the present time. Hon. gentlemen have a right to their opinion. I am giving mine and I say that the only exception I take to this change is that it is not made at a time when it will help the producer. If you are going to make the change, make it at the time when it will do the producer some good. It will not do him any good now. I have had my say and if the minister believes this is going to be beneficial, I withdraw my opposition.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: For the benefit of the hon. member, the Cereal Grain Company distributed a circular just last week stating that 80 per cent of the wheat was still in the hands of the growers.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: Might I suggest to the hon. member that the date of that letter is September 22. This is now November 7.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext:
I want to compliment the Minister of Trade and Commerce on bringing in this measure. The hon. member for South Battleford knows the practice in western Canada as well as I do and he should be willing to admit that we pool our wheat there. It has already been intimated by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that this costs us a certain amount per day. If there i3 still 50 per cent or even 30 or 25 per cent still with the growers, why should they hesitate
to take advantage of this change because they did not come in during the earlier part of the season? It will still benefit practically 50 per cent of the growers and so I congratulate the Minister of Trade and Commerce on introducing this provision.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext:
I do not want to delay the passage of this bill, but I should like to make a remark for the benefit of those members who have not been through quite as much discussion in connection with the revision of the Canada Grain Act as have some of us on this side of the house. The minister very properly says that he has every confidence in the board; so have I. The minister also says that his desire is to reduce the carrying charges on grain in storage. On that laudable object I want to compliment him. He says further that he is not prepared to discuss the details of carrying charges and so forth, and as to this I do not think he is wrong; the house cannot expect him to discuss the details. But he says we should be willing to discuss the principle and pass the bill. Let me say that no other point was more thoroughly debated and gone over than this very point when a committee of this parliament last revised the Grain Act. Members then in opposition, now sitting to the right of the Speaker, were insistent as were all members of the committee, that the whole business of handling grain, including the charges to be collected by the elevators, should be reviewed at the beginning of each crop year so that the charges could be based on a known factor. It was felt by the committee, as I recollect the matter, that it was a mistake to have rates changed at intermediate times to suit the need or exigency of some particular occasion that might arise. I can say quite frankly that such was the view of the committee and so power was left with the board, as the minister pointed out, at the beginning of the crop year to fix exactly what the elevators had a right to charge.
I want to point out this: to-day there seems to be a policy, with a low wheat market, to carry wheat. My personal view has always been that every time we have tried to carry wheat we have lost. Every year we have allowed our wheat to flow out on the markets of the world-and I am speaking not of todays' depressed market condition, but of other years-we have received the best crop prices we have ever received in the history of this country. There was a substantial opinion in this country that the pool could dictate prices to Europe. The pool, however, was unable to do so, and the American farm loan board



Canada Grain Act

could not do it by holding lip the movement of their surplus. When we are holding a large quantity of grain, as we are doing at the present time, there is no question that with elevators full, the elevators will not lose by a lowering of charges. A full elevator at the rate the minister suggests, will make money. I at present have no objection to the rate he suggests but when the situation is reversed, when the elevators are not full, when there is not much wheat in storage, what is to hinder operators from going to the board and saying: We cannot operate our elevators with only 10 per cent of our bins full; we must have a higher rate or we shall have to close up business and cease providing storage facilities? These matters were discussed in the committee as hon. members will remember and it was finally decided that the only time to revise these charges was at the beginning of the crop season.
The minister frankly says that he regrets he did not make this suggestion to the board about setting the rates at the right point at the right time and it is only because he is desirous of helping the situation that he wants this clause inserted. I want to make this suggestion to the minister. I am quite willing to admit that a benefit may accrue to the whole grain trade from lowering storage charges in the fall and winter of 1932-33, but I am not willing to admit that it is a good practice to change from the custom we have always followed, namely, of having the charges set at the beginning of the crop year. I am going to suggest to the minister that he make this bill operative for this year only, when an emergency exists, and that next year, when the charges are being set, he use his influence with the board to have them set at the correct figure. I see the present need of the suggested change; I am willing to support the bill, but after the experience we have had in revising the Canada Grain Act, due to criticism of the act, from many hon. gentlemen in the house, and after the care we took and thought we gave to the revision of this act, I do not want to see a principle, which members on both sides of the house approved and made permanent, changed although there may be need for such action this year.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext:
The hon. member for
North Bruce has just intimated in his remarks that there was a good deal of controversy over this particular section when the act was revised. I would like him and the house to recall that the desirability of fixing a rate at a given time and making no change until the end of that crop year is entirely in the

interest and at the instance of the dealer, in order that the dealer who buys or sells grain for future delivery will know that his rate of storage in the interim will not be changed. It does not affect the producer at all.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext:
My hon. friend will
admit that it helps the farmer who puts grain into storage, and many have done so.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext:
It does. My hon. friend has been arguing that no grain is in storage; that it is out of the hands of the farmer. That is just what I am arguing in regard to this bill, that it will help the farmer who has grain in hand now, but as regards the dealer who may have bought or sold grain for future delivery based on the old storage charges, it will vary the return on his investment. For that I am sorry, but I weighed the question very carefully and decided that the interest of the producer far outweighed that of the dealer who might have grain on hand or who might have sold futures or bought futures as the case might be. That was the reason I decided in that way.
Referring to my oversight in not drawing this to the attention of the board of grain commissioners at the end of the crop year, let me point out that it is the duty of the board to hear as it is the privilege of everyone interested, dealers, farmers, pool and so forth, to appear before the board and make their protests. No such protests were made, so I do not wish to leave the impression in the house that I was derelict in my duty in not bringing the matter to the attention of the board. When the matter became, as I thought, acute, the time had passed, and then I discovered the board were precluded from taking action by this particular section which we are now asking to correct.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext:
I notice this refers
to storage in public, semi-public terminal or eastern elevators under section 134. What about the storage in our country elevators under section 119? Will this apply to them and will they have to charge the same?

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: My hon. friend must not confuse section 134 with the powers of sections 15 and 17. Under sections 15 and 17 and 83 the board is given power to act in connection with feed, and it was to avoid touching these three or four different sections that I sought to amend simply one section. The board will have full power and discretion in regard to all storage charges.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext:
This simply says,
"public or semi-public terminal." It does not say anything about country elevators.


Excise Act

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: What I am asking is merely that the board shall not be precluded from making a change, which the present section 131 precludes them from doing.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: I think the minister should be congratulated upon bringing in this bill. I should not like to commit myself and say that the bill is perfect, but I think it does something that is very necessary.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: At the moment.

maintopic: CANADA GRAIN ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: GRAIN COMMISSIONERS AUTHORIZED TO REGULATE ELEVATION AND STORAGE CHARGES
speechtext: Very necessary at the moment. I think some of the charges which are now levied for handling and storing, and particularly for cleaning, should be reduced now that the price of grain is as low as it is. As far as the present board is concerned, we can trust them to see that the charges are changed in the right direction. I am very glad indeed that the bill has been brought in.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

maintopic: EXCISE ACT AMENDMENT

speechtext:
Hon. E. B. RYCKMAN (Minister of National Revenue) moved the second reading of Bill No. 7, to amend the Excise Act.
.Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. LaVergne in the chair.
On section 1-Excise duties on spirits.

maintopic: EXCISE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
This bill deals with the duties on spirits and cigarettes. The occasion for it is brought about by the agreement which was entered into with the United Kingdom. It will be noted from the schedule to the agreement that the customs duties on spirits were reduced from $10 right across the columns to $8 British preferential, making a reduction of $2 per gallon. Prior to any agreement with the United Kingdom, in fact, in the year 1930, I was waited upon by the distillers who pointed out that the excise duty, which was then $9 a gallon, was altogether too high. In 1931 they saw the department again and made the same representations. Those representations were repeated again this year before the conference was held. The customs duty having been reduced by $2 a gallon, it having stood at $10 when the excise tax was at S9 a gallon, it was thought upon consideration that the same ratio should be preserved and that the $9 excise duty should be reduced to S7. That is what the first page of this bill deals with. Frankly I am sorry to see that revenue go, but I think it will be in part made up by this fact, that we are hitting 53719-56^
the bootlegger $2 a gallon more, and his profits therefore will be $2 less. Our distillers support 25,000 people of our community. They cannot be said to be making huge profits, and it is only fair that when we make this reduction in the customs duty at the instance of the United Kingdom we should take compensatory action on behalf of those engaged in that business in this country.
Section 2 of the bill deals with allowances to be made to distillers when their product is stored. There is a slight change here, and it is being made now because it has been pressed for, and in my opinion there is reason for it. In the first place, you cannot expect, when spirits have evaporated, that the one who holds them should be called upon to pay the duty on spirits that have gone into the air, especially when he is not responsible therefor. There was an export sale for liquor in this country, especially rye and Bouibon whiskies, which were manufactured before the Export Liquor Act came into force, and now that the source of that sale has dried up, I do not think in all good conscience that we should tax evaporation. We set a standard below that of Great Britain, but in my opinion it is at least fair to the government that this change should be made.
The next and last item that the bill deals with is cigarettes. As the schedule will show, we made a change in the preferential tariff on cigarettes at the instance of representatives of the United Kingdom. That tariff was changed from $4.10 per pound and 25 per cent ad valorem to $3.50 per pound and 25 per cent ad valorem. It was thought necessary to strike a proper ratio, and it will be found, if ycu work it out, that in all cases the difference will be at least $2, depending upon whether three pounds or two and a half pounds of tobacco go into a thousand cigarettes. I believe this will not result in a great loss in revenue. In the first year there may be some loss, but I would hope that in the second year it would be made up. I believe the law of diminishing returns applies here. Due to the fact that cigarettes have been smuggled, and that many are rolling their own, the revenues from this commodity have fallen off. I believe members of the committee will be surprised to learn that 75 per cent of the fine cigarette tobacco manufactured goes into what was known as roll-your-own cigarettes. I believe that those who make their own cigarettes will :eel that they may purchase manufactured cigarettes at a reasonable cost. May I point out that all we get from that source will mean a gain of $3.40 a thousand in the amount collected by the Department of National
Excise Act

Revenue. I would hope that what might be a loss brought about by this deep cut in the tax on cigarettes will be made up at any early period through the plan suggested in the bill- cheaper cigarettes.
I can remember that my first experience in the house was in connection with the item of cigarettes. The late Mr. Fielding put a tax of 81.50 per thousand upon them and I stated that I thought the tax would result in a loss in revenue. Immediately following that he said that if such were the case the tax would be taken off. In the following year he came back and removed the tax. I now have hopes, as I told the committee, that it will work the other wayr. With our tobacco of the best quality', and our cigarettes as good as those of the United States, I believe that the private and professional bootleggers and smugglers will in a large measure be put out of business. I confidently ask the committee to support the bill. It is now brought before us because it arises through an arrangement we were asked to implement at the time of the Imperial economic conference.

maintopic: EXCISE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Perhaps I should read the titles of the different sections to be considered. First we have "Excise duties on spirits"; then, "Made from 90 per cent of unmalted grain or sugar." maintopic: EXCISE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I had intended to follow the example of the minister, and review briefly every clause in the bill. If we are now discussing only one clause I do not know whether or not I would be ruled out of order if I made some general statements.

maintopic: EXCISE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
As the minister spoke
to the whole bill I believe the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), would be justified in following his example.

maintopic: EXCISE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
Concerning the reduction in
the excise on cigarettes I favour the action taken by the minister. In fact, I hazard the opinion that he has not gone quite far enough. When some y'ears ago I had the honour of being in charge of the Department of National revenue I thought that the tax cn cigarettes was too high, and that it defeated its own purpose. That condition was brought about chiefly because of smuggling. It did not stand to reason that smuggling would not take place when men or boys could go across the border and buy cigarettes at prices ranging from twelve to fifteen cents a package, whereas in Canada the prices would be two or three times as great. The same is and was true of tobacco.

I had hoped the minister would make some adjustment concerning this commodity. For some time in the United States tobacco has been selling for from ten to fifteen cents per tin whereas in Canada one must pay from thirty cents to thirty-five cents. I am not objecting to the minister obtaining revenue, but I am inclined to believe that he is defeating his own purpose. I have no doubt there will be a continuation of smuggling of cigarettes into Canada. The minister believes that revenue which otherwise he would lose will be compensated for by' the fact that smuggling will be diminished. I am inclined to think that the reduction now under consideration, one which will be passed on by' the manufacturers to the consumers, will hardly be sufficient to discourage either smuggling or the practice of "rolling your own." I am inclined to believe that the boys will continue to roll their cigarettes, and I should have been quite happy to support him had he seen fit to make a still greater reduction.
I now direct attention to the clause dealing with the compensation to distillers for evaporation in storage of whiskies or liquors. The only point which occurs to me is this: Allowance is made for a ten-y'ear period, and provision made in the bill for an increase to fifteen years. I cannot understand why allowance should not be made so long as the liquor is in stock, no matter what the period of time may be, and according to the evaporation which may' have taken place. That, however, is merely' by the way.
Concerning the duty' on whiskey and liquor, where formerly the importers paid a duty of 810 a gallon, and the excise on the Canadian product was $9, there is now a reduction to $9 and 87 respectively. Certainly' if the minister makes a reduction in the duty on the British article it would be only' fair to the Canadian distiller to offer a similar reduction. I should like to ask the minister, however, what loss he will suffer by way of revenue; I am wondering if he has made an estimate. If the importation of liquor remains constant he must of necessity sustain a very decided loss in revenue. That is a mathematical certainty, unless compensation is made through higher consumption of liquor. I should like to know the minister's opinion in this connection. Is he going to lose revenue and, if he cares to make an estimate, how much? On the other hand, does he think compensation will be made by higher consumption -something which I should rather dislike to see. What are the minister's views in these

Excise Act
matters? I am inclined to believe that he will hardly make up the revenue by interfering with the activities of the bootleggers.

maintopic: EXCISE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I am sorry to tell the
committee that we would expect, on the basis of the current business for the twelve month period, a drop in revenues of between $7,000,000 and 88,000.000. This is a change which has been made as a result of the trade agreements. The request was made and we acceded, in an effort to fulfil our part of the bargain. Through benefits from other arrangements I hope that in time any loss will be fully made up.

maintopic: EXCISE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: My hon. friend does not anticipate eight million dollars decrease?

maintopic: EXCISE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Between seven and eight million.

maintopic: EXCISE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: Do you think they will buy more Scotch liquor instead of Canadian?

maintopic: EXCISE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
The minister has indicated that this was a matter of representation by the British representatives at the conference and that they yielded to those representations. I only wish the government had yielded to some of the representations of other interests, for instance those representing the textile industry rather than the liquor manufacturers.
The minister has also indicated that there is likely to be a loss of revenue, which from the standpoint of revenue is serious. He has expressed his opinion also that it will interfere with the bootleggers. I do not think it will, to any degree at all. I have given some consideration to this matter of the customs duty and the excise duty on liquors, and I came to this conclusion long ago, that while I do not like being placed in the position of receiving revenue from the liquor traffic, either the government or parties, as we had some discussion about a few years ago, yet we are as it were on the horns of a dilemma; we have either to make liquor cheap and increase the consumption, or make it dear and decrease the consumption and incidentally get the revenue. So I have come to this conclusion, that the best thing for Canada to do is to make liquor as dear as possible, and that way decrease consumption. I am very sorry, as I have said already, that our government saw fit to yield to the representations of the whiskey manufacturers in Great Britain rather than those of the manufacturers of woollens and cotton, boots and shoes and other things that the people need and can use without doing harm to themselves. So I can only express my regret, apart altogether from the matter of loss of revenue, that the government has seen fit to reduce the customs duty from $10 to S8 and the excise duty from $9 to $7. We admit of course that, the one having been done, the other should be done, that naturally follows. Nevertheless I cannot but feel great regret that the government has seen fit to take this position. I would also express my belief that the expectation of limiting the activities of the bootleggers will be disappointed.
As far as the clause dealing with the question of evaporation is concerned, I suppose in principle it is fair, I am not disposed to go into details on that phase. But I do not think it is good for the men or the growing boys and girls of Canada that liquor should be made any more available to them than it is at present. If this action has any effect at all it will be to increase consumption rather than decrease it, and that it is a thing to be deplored.

How does the Canadian manufacturer like that?

The importations from

the right lion, leader of the opposition is not quite correct in quoting me, I think it is even worse, that this loss of between seven and eight million dollars will fall on the spirits alone, not on spirits and cigarettes. The Canadian distiller has a municipal business tax of 150 per cent over and above the assessed value of his plant, which amounts to about $1 per case on the output of the plants. [DOT]
The British distiller has several other advantages over our manufacturers. They do

The allowance to British distillers while in warehouse continues as long as the liquors are kept in bond, 'but there is a limit on the allowance to Canadian distillers. I think it only fair that they be allowed the evaporation, as the minister suggests. The British distiller also gets 3d. a gallon on the liquor he exports, while the Canadian distiller has bo pay 3 cents a pound on the malt used in distilling.
I do not agree with the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) that the 'higher you keep the price of liquor the lower will be the consumption. I think on the other hand it will increase bootlegging and be an additional incentive to the making of home brew.

maintopic: EXCISE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I am not interested in liquor, Mr. Chairman, but I am vitally concerned in the tax on tobacco. The tobacco industry in Canada is the most highly taxed industry in the country, paying approximately $46,000,000 to the federal treasury each year. I should like to ask the minister if he would accept an amendment to this section, because I believe this government is ready and willing to do whatever it can for the fanner.

maintopic: EXCISE ACT AMENDMENT

A foolish fellow always laughs when he has nothing on his mind. The situation in the tobacco areas of western Ontario is deplorable. Section 3 reads:
(f) on cigarettes made from raw leaf tobacco or any substitute therefor, weighing not more than three pounds per thousand, four dollars per thousand.
I suggest to the minister that this be amended to read as follows:
(f) on cigarettes made from raw leaf tobacco grown and processed in Canada, weighing not more than three pounds per thousand, four dollars per thousand.
I might explain to the hon. gentlemen opposite who laughed a moment ago that every time they smoke a cigarette-

maintopic: EXCISE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext: I do not smoke cigarettes.

maintopic: EXCISE ACT AMENDMENT

If that is a compliment you are welcome to it. The tax on a single cigarette is six-tenths of one cent, or $6 per thousand on all cigarettes weighing less than three pounds to the thousand, while it is $11 on cigarettes weighing more than three pounds to the thousand. The cigarette smokers of Canada contribute $30,000,000 a year to the federal treasury. The ex-Minister of National Revenue said the reduction was not sufficient to suit him. I hope he was not serious, because this reduction is $2 per thousand more than we were able to get during the nine years the Liberals were in power. I do not care the snap of my fingers for those who roll their own cigarettes; all I am interested in is having Canadian tobacco used in Canadian cigarettes which are consumed by Canadian smokers. It has been stated-and it may be quite correct-that each year a billion cigarettes are smuggled into this country from the United States, and the approximate annual consumption of cigarettes in Canada amounts to about five billion.
I agree with the ex-minister when he says that a reduction in the excise duty will bring about a falling off in revenue. The United States had the same experience a few years ago, when they reduced the excise tax on cigarettes from $6 to $3 per thousand. Naturally their revenue fell off, but within five years the output and consumption -of cigarettes had doubled, making up for the .previous loss in revenue. I contend that while we may lose money in revenue this year, and possibly for another year or two as well, within five jmars the consumption and output of cigarettes in Canada will have doubled. This means a good deal to the Canadian grower of tobacco, and I do humbly suggest to the minister that he accept the amendment I have offered.

maintopic: EXCISE ACT AMENDMENT
speechtext:
I cannot agree with the hon. member. What about the health of the minors of Canada? Is that to 'be ruined? What about the growing populace of this country? If you double the production and the use of cigarettes you can see what the results will be. One has only to walk down the street and look at the sidewalks paved with half-smoked cigarettes to see where the waste is taking place in Canada. We could pay off the national debt with the money that is consumed in cigarette smoke. I am absolutely opposed to anything that would increase the consumption of cigarettes in this

speechtext:
Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) moved the second reading of Bill No. 4, respecting a certain trade agreement between the Dominion of Canada and the Irish Free State.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. LaVergne in the chair.
Sections 1 to 4, inclusive, agreed to.
On the schedule.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE IRISH FREE STATE
speechtext: With regard to the schedule, I observe that for the most part its purpose is to secure both the Irish Free State and Canada against duties being raised against each other. It is protection as against the raising of duties on the part of either country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE IRISH FREE STATE
speechtext:
I do not think the right hon. gentleman has followed the language of the schedule. The first article reads:
Goods the produce or manufacture of Canada, imported into the Irish Free State, shall not be subject to other or higher duties than those paid on similar goods, the produce or manufacture of any other country.
	,
In other words, no more favourable terms can be accorded any other country than to Canada. Then, so far as the complementary article is concerned, it provides:
Goods, the produce or manufacture of the Irish Free State, imported into Canada, shall not be subject to other or higher duties than those paid on similar goods, the produce or manufacture of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and ^Northern Ireland.
That is to say, the British preference expressed in terms of duties charged against goods of the United Kingdom and Northern Ireland. In other words, if duties were increased by Great Britain then the rates here might be made similar to those, and if the rates charged by the Irish Free State against the country at the present time enjoying the most favoured terms were increased, the same action might be taken with respect to Canadian goods; the standard being in one case the most favourable terms granted by the Irish Free State to any other country, and the standard in the other case being the duties charged by Canada against goods from the United Kingdom or from Northern Ireland.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE IRISH FREE STATE
speechtext: It may be said, however, that, generally speaking, the emphasis is on the protection of each country against higher duties, rather than-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE IRISH FREE STATE
speechtext: No. I think I can put it fairly by saying that it does not do either one or the other. It does, however, secure this preference to Canada, <that we shall receive the benefits of the lowest rates imposed by the Irish Free State; and, conversely, we afford to them the rates, whatever they may be, charged against the United Kingdom and Northern Ireland.

Schedule agreed to.
On section 5-Suspension of inconsistent laws.

The operation of all laws inconsistent with the giving to the provisions of the said agreement and of this act their full effect shall from time to time be suspended to the extent of such inconsistency.
The Minister of Justice will put it in better form, and the committee might rise and report progress and ask leave to sit again, possibly this day.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND SOUTHERN RHODESIA
speechtext: This clause refers to the schedule to the bill. Will my right hon. friend kindly indicate just what the schedule really signifies? It is difficult to make much out of the reading of it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND SOUTHERN RHODESIA
speechtext:
I think I can do that in not too many words. It follows the usual form so far as the provision relating to our customs tariff is concerned; that is the general provisions of our tariff are, as my right hon. lriend will see from article I, not suspended or abrogated. Then we provide:
(a)	goods the produce or manufacture of southern Rhodesia, enumerated in schedule \ to this agreement, shall, when imported direct into Canada, enjoy the benefits of the tariff concessions indicated in the said schedule;
(b)	all other goods, the produce or manufacture of Southern Rhodesia, shall when imported direct into Canada, enjoy the benefits of the British preferential tariff.
In other words, article I of the agreement contemplates certain Southern Rhodesian goods receiving better than the British preferential treatment, and those that do not receive better than the British preferential treatment, will receive the British preferential treatment. That number, as the right hon. member will observe from schedule A, is very limited. It includes:
Indian corn, n.o.p.
Grape fruit, when imported from the place of growth by ship, direct to a Canadian port.
Oranges.
Lemons.
Limes.
Peanuts, green, in the shell or not further processed than shelled.
Peanuts receive the same treatment as we accord in the case of Australia. That we thought to be ample, as it is covered by a treaty.
The rest of the goods other than those that come within the specifications of schedule A are to receive the benefits of the British preferential treatment. It will be observed, however, that the complementary side of it is contained in article II. I will not take up time explaining or reading it because, as I see, the committee is thoroughly familiar with it. But article III reads:
1.	Goods, the produce or manufacture of Southern Rhodesia, enumerated in schedule A to this agreement, shall, on importation into Canada, enjoy -the benefits of the lowest rates of customs duty applicable to similar goods imported from any country.
That makes it quite clear again that the goods enumerated in schedule A enjoy the benefits of the lowest rates of customs duty applicable to similar goods imported from any country.
Section 2 of article III reads:
2.	Similarly, goods, the produce or manufacture of Canada, enumerated in schedule B to this agreement, shall, on importation into Southern Rhodesia, enjoy the benefit of the lowest rates of customs duty applicable to similar goods imported from any country.
Schedule B will be found on page 4. It will be observed that they comprise not a large number of items. They include:
Cream separators.
Batteries.
Boots and shoes.
Boxes.
Wood.
The two latter items cover the timber business.
Paper.
Another branch of the lumber industry. The details I apprehend the committee has read. There was, however, one difficulty. Those who are familiar with the geography of Southern Rhodesia will know that it is a longer distance from Southern Rhodesia to ports in South Africa than it is immediately to the ocean across intervening Portuguese territory. It will be observed that these words in clause 3 of the bill cover that situation:
3.	After the said agreement is brought into force, and so long as it remains in force, goods, the produce or manufacture of Southern

Rhodesia, conveyed, without transhipment, from a port of any British country enjoying the benefits of the British preferential tariff, or any lower tariff, or from the nearest seaport accessible to Southern Rhodesia, into a sea, lake or river port of Canada, shall be admitted to Canada at the rates of duties provided in the said agreement.
In other words, that is regarded as a direct shipment, As a matter of fact the port, Beira, as I remember it, is distant from Rhodesia only about 100 miles, whereas it is 600 miles or more to reach the other port.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND SOUTHERN RHODESIA
speechtext: Can my right hon. friend indicate in a general way the extent of Canada's trade with Rhodesia?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND SOUTHERN RHODESIA
speechtext:
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has the figures; I have not them beside me at the moment. The trade is not very considerable, but it shows signs of possible improvement. For instance, Rhodesia produces Indian corn rather extensively. So far as grape fruit is concerned, it will secure a place in our market at a time when the other British possessions supplying that commodity would not be competing. The same may be said with respect to oranges, lemons and limes.
With regard to the items mentioned in schedule B the trade promises very substantial improvement in what one might call the lumber or timber items. On boxes it will be observed there is a five per cent preference in favour of Canada. On wood they give us the most favoured nation clause. As regards paper we have a preference on newsprint in reels or in the flat, 10 per cent ad valorem. That promises to be a trade that might be fairly expanded. On the other paper items w'e have a 10 per cent preference. On wrapping paper there is a 10 per cent preference and the same with respect to a special kind of wrapping paper which they carry in their schedule in a particular manner, namely, for wrapping fruit. I think it fair to say that the general preference is 10 per cent on the lumber items and products of lumber except boxes, where it is five per cent. On boots and shoes the preference is 10 per cent ad valorem duty for ours and a 15 per cent advantage, making it a 25 per cent tariff against foreign countries. With respect to electrical batteries, the preference against foreign countries is 15 per cent although our items are taxable five per cent. I do not carry in mind the exact volume of trade. I asked my colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, to get it and he informs me the papers are on their way, and he will give the figures to the committee at an early moment.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA

speechtext:
Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) moved the second reading of Bill No. 3, respecting a certain trade agreement between the Dominion of Canada and the Union of South Africa.
Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING
{Leader of the Opposition): I notice that article IV of the schedule attached to this agreement provides that:
His Majesty's government in the Dominion of Canada will, in regard to the goods enumerated in schedule "A," maintain the margins of tariff concession represented by the difference between the rates accorded to Union goods in that schedule and the presently existing rates on similar goods when imported* from any foreign country.
Under that article the government is asking us to bind ourselves to maintain certain rates of the general tariff for the period of the agreement, a period of five years. I wish to say that I think the parliament of Canada should be free at all times to alter its tariff in any respect that it desires, and that we should not bind ourselves to maintain a certain tariff rate, even if it is fixed only so as to continue a margin of preference; but subsequent parliaments, or the same parliament at subsequent sessions, should at all times be free to alter rates of duty in any and every particular. My right hon. friend will probably say, "we are binding ourselves only in honour," that "of course parliament is supreme at all times." But while he may bind himself in honour to maintain a certain tariff rate with l-espeet to commodities coming into this country, I, as representing the Liberal party in Canada, cannot bind myself in honour to maintain any tariff rates so long as I may be of the opinion that at some subsequent time the people of Canada may desire to have those rates changed. I want to take this first opportunity of emphasizing what I feel to be a very grave objection to this particular phase of this agreement, a phase which is to be found in some of the other agrements as well. The tariff schedule is a very lai'ge one; we have had no opportunity whatever of discussing it, and I question very much
if the Prime Minister will allow us an opportunity of going into committee of ways and means before this second reading is disposed of, or even after it is disposed of, to discuss item by item the several articles mentioned in the schedule. And without going very carefully through that schedule I submit it is impossible for this house to say to what extent it is binding itself with respect to the maintenance of certain protective rates of duty for the next five yeai's. I realize that the government have bound themselves to carry this agi'eement through, and they probably will do so by the strength of their majority in the house. But I should be entirely lacking in appi'eciation of what I feel is owing to the other party to the agreement if I did not make it perfectly clear that as far as the Liberal party is concerned we intend to assert and maintain the principle that parliament is supreme at all times with respect to all matters, and to none more than those which concern taxation, and that at any time we feel it to be in the public interest that rates of duty should be changed, we, should we be exercising authority at the time, will not regard ourselves as bound in that particular by anything that appears in the agreements in the form in which they are.
