speakeroldname: Hon. H. H. STEVENS (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
The right hon. gentleman has raised a point which he 'has laboured I think on previous occasions, complaining in regard to certain provisions of this treaty. It will be observed that the government of the Union of South Africa also undertakes to maintain the margin of preference created in schedule B to Canadian goods over similar goods when imported from any foreign country. I think the house should bear in mind in dealing particularly with this agreement that the Union of South Africa in its policy regarding trade matters has not followed the same course that we have in Canada. Instead of giving a certain preference- say a British preference-as we do on all goods, they limit the goods on 'which Great Britain is entitled to a special preference to a certain, list. And they have done the same thing with us. Their practice is this, that when they do fix a list which seems to be most suitable to the part of the empire to which it is extended, the preference is limited to the country to which that list is applied. In this case Canada gets a preference on a certain list of articles which in our estimation are the most advantageous to our trade, and that list is not extended to other countries. That is the principle upon which they have carried on their trade. South Africa said to us: "We will maintain this preference for you, but you must maintain the preference on the limited list that you extend to us." It is on that limited list that this preference is extended. As to the right hon. gentleman's reference to the list as a large one, it is not a very large list. There are probably about twenty-five items in it, out of a tariff list of some 900 or 1,000 items. So it is not a very large list, but it includes items that are typical of Canadian trade.
It might be well for me at this point to deal with the way in which Canadian trade with South Africa has developed. It will be recalled that the Union of South Africa, origin-

ally the four colonies, established in 1903 a preferential ad valorem rebate to the United Kingdom, of three per cent on most of their goods. This was not applicable to all their goods. It was extended to Canada because we had extended British preferential tariff treatment to South African goods. In 1925 South Africa discontinued this uniform three per cent ad valorem rebate and adopted a tariff with columns of maximum and minimum duties, although on many items maximum and minimum rates were the same. In 1925 they adopted a new policy, and that is the tariff system which is now in force. The preference allocated to Canada in 1925, following this adjustment of their tariff system, conceded the minimum tariff to Canada on wheat, wheat flour, preserved fish, hosiery, binder twine, pipe and fittings of iron and steel, cocks, taps, meters, electrical cooking and heating appliances, mechanics' tools, white lead, rubber tires and tubes, newsprint and unmanufactured wood. It is only on these goods that a tariff preference is now granted to Canada by the Union of South Africa. The new agreement retains the former preferences, gives increased preference on two items, provides new preferences on ten, and secures to Canada the most favoured nation treatment on fifteen other items. This was considered a very valuable extension of privilege for Canadian trade in the South African market. As complained of by the right hon. leader of the opposition, we have undertaken on a certain limited list to maintain the preference, and South Africa has undertaken correspondingly on a similar limited list of Canadian articles to maintain the preference, or the margin, in that market.
I confess that I cannot follow my right hon. friend in the alarm he expresses as to the adoption, as he calls it, of this principle. I think that very largely, if not absolutely, we were similarly bound in connection with the French treaty. At least we were in this position, that we fixed certain duties under the French treaty that we could not change, and that were accorded to twenty-three other countries by virtue of the most favoured nation provision; and we were without power to change that unless we abrogate the treaty.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: Six months' notice was all that was required.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
But we had to abrogate the whole treaty to do it. I think the house ought to pause in this controversy that has been going on for the last two or three weeks to consider the significance of that. My right bon. friend takes refuge, shall I say, in the fact that six months' notice was provided in the French treaty. But surely when we enter

South Africa

into a treaty we do not expect that if there are some items in it that do not quite suit us or do not come up to our expectations, within a few days we will abrogate the treaty, because that is the only remedy. In all these treaties, while we have fixed a period of five years and have adopted certain provisions with regard to the maintenance of a spread, there is the spirit of adjustment and compromise by consultation. There is present an entirely different atmosphere from that which we find in the ordinary treaty between two foreign countries, and I think that should be borne in mind. There is nothing alarming in this matter of maintaining a spread; the items are comparatively few.
Another point about which my right hon. friend complains is this: a moment ago he intimated -that he did not suppose the Prime Minister would allow the house to examine these schedules in committee of ways and means. Let us look at that question very frankly. The British treaty and the treaty under consideration have been presented to the house in a normal manner. We come to the house and say: "We have entered into agreements with Great Britain, with Southern Rhodesia, with the Irish Free State and with South Africa. We now bring forward these bills, by which we ask the house to ratify our action." Then what happens? The bill is read a first time in the ordinary course. It is presented to the house and read a second time. By giving the bill that second reading the house approves of the general principle of entering into an agreement. Then we go into committee of the whole on the bill and the schedules. In committee of the whole we can examine every item, every figure, every letter, the dotting of every "i" and the crossing of every "t". There is nothing we cannot examine, and the fullest information desired by the house may and will be given. Having gone through that procedure we give the bill third reading, but still the measure is not complete. It is still open; i-t must go to the other house, where it is given similar treatment. There is not an item affecting the tariff that we are not competent to examine while a bill is going through that process, precisely as we examine these items in the committee of ways and means. What is that committee for? It is simply to regularize all these agreements in the nomenclature of the tariff, to harmonize the provisions of the bill with the general tariff provisions. That is what the committee of ways and means is for.
I submit that my right hon. friend is doing himself and the public an injustice when he seeks to leave the impression that because we
do not go into committee of ways and means on something we have not yet ratified, we are doing an injustice to this house. I submit this to the right hon. gentleman: having gone through these processes we send the bill to the other house. Mark you, the ratification is not complete until the bill passes the other house and gets royal assent, but we send the bill out of here; then we go into committee of ways and means, and go through the whole process again. If we went into committee of ways and means before passing the bill it would be similar to putting the cart before the horse; we would be amending the tariff, harmonizing it with something we had not considered. I wonder if my right hon. friend has thought of that. Here we have measures which he says we should not consider at all; he says we should just lay them aside and adjust the tariff in accordance with these agreements. If we are not going to ratify the agreements after full examination, there is no need to make the amendments to the tariff; of course, in that case the whole thing is wiped out.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: Did I understand the minister to say that we cannot go into committee of ways and means until the bills have passed the Senate?

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
No, we do not wait until they have passed the Senate; as soon as they go from this house we proceed in an orderly way to harmonize what we have done with the general tariff, in the ways and means committee. If we did otherwise we would be putting the cart before the horse. We simply work into this schedule of more than one thousand items, which we call our tariff, the adjustments that we make in these agreements, and if we are to follow the ordinary precedents of this house the agreements first must be passed.
Perhaps I have gone into this matter a little more than is necessary, but twice this afternoon and on previous occasions as well my right hon. friend has suggested that we are not treating the house fairly in asking the house to consider these agreements first. I invite the right hon. gentleman to the most careful scrutiny of these schedules. A moment ago my hon. friend from Quebec West asked a question with regard to one of the items, and he found that we simply sought to harmonize that item with the general tariff schedule. It is highly technical and narrow, if you like, but these things must be done and they can be done only in the committee of the whole.

My right hon. friend said we had not all the information before us. I am reminded that at least since Friday, October 7, the full list of items and all the amendments to the Tariff Act and the tariff schedule have been before the house, not those affecting just one treaty but all the necessary changes, covering every item cited in all the agreements. Not only is that the case; in these lists we have also given the old and the new rates, and I am sure that on second thought the right hon. gentleman will realize that every possible bit of information has been given the house that could be given. Now we are here prepared to analyze the schedules in detail. I invite my right hon. friend to join with us in scrutinizing these items. We are prepared to discuss them. Of course we hope that we will be able to satisfy any reasonable member of the house that each item has been carefully considered before being agreed to. Each one has been gone into with great care, and we are sure we will be able to meet the reasonable requirements of any hon. member in this connection.
I should like to come back for a moment, however, to the point stressed by the right hon. gentleman, that there is something that does violence to his sense of parliamentary practice and to his ideas of constitutional procedure, in guaranteeing to South Africa a spread on a limited number of items. Let me remind the house that South Africa has given us the same guarantee, and that guarantee is more important to us than is our guarantee to South Africa. I may assure hon. gentlemen of that. So we submit to the house that there are no grounds for objection, constitutionally, in practice or in equity, to this method of procedure. We leave it, then, to the judgment of the house.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
I wish
to recall to the house what happened in connection with the Australian treaty. That treaty, it will be remembered, was made in October, and it got into this house when parliament opened in January or February, but nothing more was heard of the treaty. No details of that treaty came to this house until three days before prorogation. It was discussed in this house for three days.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: What year?

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
I think it was in 1925.
The leader of the government of that day thought that three days was enough to discuss that treaty, right on the eve of prorogation. It is an entirely different matter now. It is true this is a more important treaty, but I have seen no evidence of any desire

on anyone's part to limit discussion. There has been no limit of discussion on the other side, heaven knows. Let hon. gentlemen stop and think what happened then and what is happening now. My hon. friend also speaks of the French treaty as if it were some paragon of virtue. They kept it in force for ten years, and it should have been abrogated in six months. The first is in relation to the suggestion or the fact that under the terms of these treaties this parliament is bound for five years to maintain certain definite schedules, certain definite tariffs, certain definite spreads in the tariff schedules, and so this parliament is unable to deal with its own tariff in relation to other countries and to make treaties into which we might otherwise enter. I am assuming that these treaties are not imperial in the true sense of the word; that is, they are not an integral part of an imperial policy; but that each one is a separate treaty which has to do almost wholly with the two countries which are vitally concerned; that it is possible at all times to vary the terms of that treaty up or down if the two countries mainly concerned agree on the changes which should be made. But there is another point, and it is one which has given me some concern. We have heard a good deal about the restriction of the right of parliament to deal as it felt inclined with its taxation policy, its tariff and all the other matters, the right, the freedom of parliament at all times to do exactly what it likes and to maintain its own inherent control over its policy. But at the same time we have heard a great deal of 'another subject, namely, the necessity of international cooperation and agreement by means of which we should have a substantial lowering of tariffs amongst all countries. It seems to me that you cannot have absolute individual freedom, whether of man or of nation, coupled with a policy of complete cooperation. As soon as you begin to cooperate, whether that cooperation is between individuals or nations, to the extent of your cooperation, you must surrender your individual right or freedom. To me at least, it seems wholly contradictory, wholly impossible, to talk about international cooperation, future international agreements and world action for a common end, and at the same time to insist that at all times and under all circumstances we in this country and in this parliament must retain our individual right to act exactly as we please. You cannot have those two things together. Because I am so firmly convinced that the future of the world rests much more upon cooperation than it does upon the individual right of every country to act as it sees fit, I for one would be willing to surrender a good deal of our right to deal with our own private affairs as we wish, if in surrendering that we were able to lead the way or take part in world cooperation towards world recovery. But, as I say, you cannot have the two together. I was brought up in the old MJanchester school of free trade and individualism. I have not lost my feeling towards free trade if it is world-wide, but I have become convinced that we have long passed the stage when the school of individualism has a leg left to stand on, and we have to surrender such individualism, whether as a man or a nation, in order to cooperate

There is the issue plain and simple. We say that it has been the considered policy of statesmen of the British empire for a period of years commencing before 1917 to endeavour to maintain and support the policy of friendly trade relations between the dominions, and that we have felt that that is the best way to ensure stability in our own trade, permanency in our fiscal relations, so that we would not be subject to what happened to Canada a few short years ago. I saw the entire ranching industry of western Canada practically destroyed by the Fordney-McCumber tariff. I saw a gentleman who measured his wealth by millions ruined completely. W'hy? Because the United States enacted a new tariff law after the Wilson tariff that completely destroyed our ranching population. If the right hon. gentleman would ask the banks what their losses were in connection with these matters; if he would ask the individuals who found themselves insolvent by reason of it, he, I think, would quite agree that it is highly desirable that somewhere within this world we should have a channel of trade that would not be subject to the whims of an election, the mere caprice of the day. That is what we have done; that is what we have endeavoured to prevent. We had free wheat, we had free cattle, we had free lumber and grains, and the Fordney-McCumber tariff ended that, and did a tremendous injury to our people. We had lumber at a given rate; the other day a foreign country suddenly placed a higher tariff against it, with great injury to our people.

such, is for twelve years. That was brought forward as a family arrangement, because we desired to assist our brethren in the West Indies, and did so. Both parties in this house accepted that treaty. It is true that it involved a loss of $1,000,000 a year to the Dominion of Canada, because of the obligations we incurred, but no one complained because it was a family arrangement.
This, too, is a family arrangement with South Africa; we have told them that for five years we will maintain the status quo in order to enable trade to be maintained; in order to enable us to find markets there to meet the requirements of our trade, and in order to enable them to find markets here for the requirements of their trade. It is for that reason that we seek the term of five years. Many people think that term too short; many people think a term of five years will not enable the greatest advantages and benefits to be derived from this agreement. At any rate it is for that period and, as I say, that is in addition to the fact that this is a family arrangement; in addition to the desire to obtain secure markets and clear-cut channels of trade upon which we can depend, so that we will not be subject to the caprices and whims of people not within the empire, by which our fiscal fife may be destroyed at a moment's notice, and by which the individual may find himself ruined through the sudden change of tariffs by a foreign country. We have chosen to prefer our kinsmen within the empire to the foreigner without, and upon that we stand or fall; upon that this government stands or falls.
We still believe-and I have heard no argument that in any sense touches the question-that it is highly desirable that this country should know that it has a fixed and certain market embracing a quarter of the population of the world, a market that will not be taken from it as the result of a general election in any particular part of the empire, and that there will be a constant opportunity during a period of five years, with the ebb and flow of trade to establish a channel that, if it succeeds, will be perpetuated. If it fails it will be terminated.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
The Prime Minister says I am taking the position that I favour trade agreements between Canada and foreign countries but that I do not favour trade agreements between Canada and other parts of the British Empire. There could be no possible misrepresentation of my attitude greater than that. I have repeatedly said there is everything to be said for trade agreements between different parts of the empire, (Mr. Bennett.]
provided that those trade agreements do not restrict or prevent us from making trade agreements with other countries of the world which may be ito the advantage of Canada, and which being to -the advantage of Canada I claim will also be of advantage to the British Empire. These agreements go much further than simply affording to other parts of the empire an opportunity to trade in Canada on certain terms. If the agreement under discussion simply gave South Africa a preference in our market I would have much less to say about the five year period for which the agreement is to run. Give to the countries of the British Empire an opportunity to trade in our market under a preference afforded through a lowering of tariffs and I will not quarrel greatly with hon. gentlemen opposite over any length of time they wish to have such an agreement run.
That is not the situation here, Mr. Speaker. Under the guise of a family agreement the government is asking us first to raise the tariff against foreign countries and then to agree to maintain the tariff against foreign countries at the very high level which the margin of preference may necessitate its remaining at a margin which may be prejudicial to the great consuming and producing portions of the country, and in many cases to the manufacturing interests of Canada as well. In connection with these agreements we also must remember how inordinately high our tariff is at the present tiime, and how it came to be at such a level. It is not the tariff which my right hon. friend inherited when he came into power in 1930. In the fall of that year the tariff which existed at that -time was increased against Great Britain as well as against foreign countries. That tariff was further raised in 1931, and last session it was increased yet again. It is higher -than ever now by virtue of certain interpretations which have been put upon legislation passed and by other features of its administration, and it is that particular tariff-at inordinate heights-which in some cases is being lowered to a very slight extent but -which is so fixed by marginal preferences as to maintain a very considerable protection against foreign countries during the entire life of these agreements. This is not a family feature at all. As I said before, the family feature which obtains where a preference is given through a reduction of tariffs is all to the good, but when apart from this you ask us so to fix our tariffs that we cannot trade with other countries during that period of time on any terms under which we may wish to trade with them, you create quite a different situation.

South Africa
Let me put this in the clearest possible terms. As I read them, these treaties or agreements are not so much treaties for the purpose of promoting trade within the British Empire-which is a very laudable end, and the purpose which hon. gentlemen opposite are putting forward-as they are treaties to make more difficult trade between different parts of the British Empire, and Canada in particular, and the other countries of the world. That is exactly the case, and an examination of the treaties will confirm that statement. May I point out that there is a school of imperialists who believe that this is the right thing to do, and I do not hesitate to say that the Prime Minister belongs to that school. He believes that is the very thing he is doing. I believe hon. gentlemen opposite may be thoroughly honest and sincere in their point of view, When the Prime Minister says that he believes the way to bring about a consolidated British Empire is by tariffs which will make difficult trade with other parts of the world he is only saying what Mr. Hewins says in the book which the Prime Minister quoted the other day; he is only saying what Richard Jebb has said in his treaties on the imperial conferences, he is only saying what hundreds of other imperialist protectionists have said is the best way of securing a consolidated empire. My view of what is best for the future of the British Empire, however, is that it does not lie in the direction of a consolidation which will lead to the centralization of government and the adoption thereby of imperial policies for the empire as a whole. I believe that the conception of the British Empire as reached at the imperial conference of 1926, which has found its expression in the statute of Westminster passed this very year, and which looks upon each part of the empire as a self-governing community, sovereign in its fiscal and all other rights is the only true conception. I believe that on this basis the British Empire will last, but I say that the moment you try to bring about a consolidated empire by way of tariffs which restrict its parts from trading with other parts of the world, at that moment you begin [DOT]to create a kind of protection that will help [DOT]destroy the empire. The British Empire has been founded on freedom, not restraint, and the whole evolution of the empire has been through getting rid of restraints, political and [DOT]otherwise, and making each part of the empire free to determine its own policies.
Hon. gentlemen opposite seek now to reverse the whole process and, by this system of tariffs, make it increasingly difficult for this country, as a part of the British Empire, to
[DOT]trade with other countries. If we are called [DOT]upon as members of parliament to consider these matters, having considered their ill effects, desire to change any schedule, then we [DOT]are charged with disloyalty to the other parts of the British Empire. I say that is not a [DOT]fair or right position in which to put this-country or this parliament in relation to other [DOT]parts of the empire.
My right hon, friend quoted a resolution which was passed in 1917, at an imperial conference held in London in that year, which, resolution declared that every effort should be made to develop the resources and industries of the different countries of the empire in such a way as would help to make the empire independent of other parts of the world. He says that we are going counter to that resolution and adds that I was a party to the approving of it. Does anyone fancy that I would have approved of that had I thought that it would be construed as meaning that the only way in which the British empire could be made independent of other parts of the world was by means of tariffs which would render it impossible for Canada to carry on trade with other countries? That is the interpretation he places upon the resolution,, and that is the trouble with my right hon. friend and others who think as he does. They think altogether in terms of protection and protection alone. They cannot conceive of the possibility of a great British Empire founded upon freedom, above all freedom of trade, notwithstanding the fact that Britain has reached her present prominence through decades of fiscal freedom and freedom of trade. If I w^ere to express my own mind I should say that in my belief every portion of the empire would develop more fully and would promote the development of a greater empire, as a whole, and the empire would become more independent of the rest of the world,' if all its component parts along with other nations were free to develop their own industries in the way they deemed best, regardless altogether of tariffs.
There are many ways in which the industries of a country can be built up, apart from tariffs. Indeed, I believe that tariffs have done as much to destroy the industries of countries as they have done to help to create industries.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: Why keep them?

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
They have done this for the reason that under protection capital has been diverted into channels that have been relatively unproductive, whereas under a system of free competition such capital
906	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
would have gone into industries which the country was best adapted to develop, and the point would have been reached long ere this where the countries of the empire would have been largely independent of others. That is the significance which I attach to that resolution of 1917-preference within empire by the lowering, not the raising of tariffs,-and which I attached to it at the time it was under discussion at the imperial conference to which my hon. friend has referred. That resolution was accepted, not because of its wording or of any interpretation that could be put upon it by those who were politically opposed. I took care to inquire into the significance of the terms and I state again that if I had thought for a moment that there would have been put upon that resolution such an interpretation as that which my right hon. friend seeks to put upon it at the present time, I would certainly not have agreed to it. My hon. friend asks, what about some wealthy individual who lost a huge fortune at a shot because of the Fordney-McCumber tariff? I ask him, What about the thousands and hundreds of thousands of people who to-day are finding it difficult to obtain food, clothing and shelter-the people who under these agreements which are before the house are going to be compelled to continue the payment of a toll not only to the country in the form of taxes, but to the textile and other industries as well, in the form of dividends and profits? These are the people about whom I am concerned. The individuals who possess vast estates and great -wealth will be able to look after themselves. But when you ask us to bind Canada for five years to some of the high tariffs fixed in these schedules, then I say that the time has come to inquire how these schedules will affect the hundreds of thousands of consumers in this country, who are finding it difficult to get food, clothing and shelter and all the necessities that are affected adversely by the height of these tariffs.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
The right hon. gentleman has focussed his persistent opposition to these agreements mainly upon two points; one is the five year period, and allied -with that, he says, is the fact that we are binding this country in a certain limited list of items to a fixed preference. That is to say, we are binding ourselves to maintain a tariff, a general tariff or an intermediate, of an amount equal to that preference at lea*. And he cites that as a reason for the bitter opposition to this and the other agreements. He says it is a violation of principle and, in his recent remarks as in several speeches he has delivered,

he declares that it is a very serious departure from the best known' principles of governmental procedure.
I have here the West India Treaty, article 2 of which reads:
Subject to the provisions of the Customs Tariff, 1907, the Dominion of Canada grants to the articles enumerated in schedule A, being the produce or manufacture of any of the colonies aforesaid, when imported into Canada, the preferential treatment indicated, in respect of each such article, in the said schedule A.
That is the first provision which I would cite from that treaty. Then in article 20 I find that:
This agreement shall remain in force for twelve years, and thereafter-
And so forth. Then I look at schedule A and I find, with respect to sugar of polarization of 96 degrees-the degrees vary up or down from that point, but 96 is the point at Which the greatest quantity is imported-that we undertake to maintain a preference of $1 per hundred pounds. Now, my right hon. friend has just been shedding crocodile tears with regard to the food) of the poor; but he, himself, bound Canada-and we are still bound

for a period of twelve years to maintain in this country a tariff of at least $1 per hundred pounds, or one cent per pound, on sugar.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: It has been raised since.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: And that provision is there yet; you could not depant from it. It binds our hands, just as my right hon. friend remained bound all the time he was in power. We are still bound by it.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: Where is sugar now?

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
Precisely where it was
then.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: No; you raised it by order in council.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
My hon. friend is not
going to get me away from the point I am discussing. I shall in a moment state what changes, if any, have been made. I will have it looked up, but I do not believe there were any changes. The point I am making, however, is that under this agreement the right hon. gentleman bound the parliament of Canada for twelve years to maintain a tariff of at least SI per hundred pounds on sugar. As a matter of fact, it was in this agreement that the general tariff was fixed at SI per hundred pounds above that of the West Indies. I find that bananas were made free to the West Indies as against a general

South Africa
tariff of 50 cents. Tlie right hon. gentleman bound us there again, on fruit for the pool people of Canada, to the extent of 50 cents per bunch. I come now to cocoa beans- someone mentioned cocoa beans as the food of the poor because it was cheap; this statement was made in the debate the other day. In regard to cocoa beans, roasted or crushed, the preference per hundred pounds is SI .50 intermediate and |2 under the general. The food of the poor! For twelve years the right hon. gentleman tied the hands of this parliament. Lime juice, we find, carries a preference of 15 cents per gallon, and limes are free as against a general tariff of 15 cents. What a terrible thing to put in a statute! He tells us that for twelve years we must maintain a tariff of 15 cents. I come now to arrowroot, which is the food of the sick and invalids: free as against a general tariff of 14 cents per pound. Then we have cocoa-nut free as against a general tariff of 75 cents per 100 pounds; grape fruit, a preference of SI under the general tariff. This is the language of this agreement under which my right hon. friend tied our hands for twelve years. On rum-and let me draw the attention of the hon. member for Lisgar to this- his leader tied the hands of this parliament with a preference of $2 per gallon, proof strength. Onions

I suppose that is the food of the rich-free as against a general tariff of 30 per cent. The hands of parliament were bound for twelve years with a tariff of 30 per cent. Cocoa butter free as against a general tariff of two cents a pound. Coffee, green, free as against a tariff of three cents per pound. Think of tying the hands of parliament for twelve years by imposition of a duty of three cents a pound on coffee! That is scandalous. Ginger and spices, free as against a general tariff of 124 per cent. Pineapples, fixed at one-half cent. Sponges, free as against a general tariff of 174 per cent. In order to make the matter doubly clear this provision is made:
Provided that nothing herein contained shall prevent the government of Canada from changing the rates of duty provided the preference* granted herein are maintained.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: That is the whole story.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
There was nothing wrong
in tying the hands of parliament for twelve years, nothing wrong in tying the hands of Canada for twelve years on sugar, beyond doubt an important item of daily household use; nothing in the world wrong with that, but, my! what a terrible thing this government is now doing in dealing with the mother
country and South Africa! I find some very illustrious names signed to this agreement: the Right Hon. George P. Graham, now in the Senate; and two others who have passed away, the late Mr. Robb and the late Mr. Low; the Hon. W. R. Motherwell, Mr. John E. Sinclair, who has been translated to the other house; the Hon. P. J. A. Cardin, now in the front benches opposite, then a member of the government.
Some of these gentlemen, still with us, are voting to condemn this government and to put it out of office because it makes a treaty with the mother country for five years and fixes a preference on a certain list of articles, yet these gentlemen bound the country for twelve years in precisely the same way. I am not quarrelling with the right hon. gentleman for doing what he did; not at all. But what I say is this: What degree of confidence can anyone in this house or out of it put in the sincerity of the right hon. gentleman now? Does he think he has added an iota to this debate by the attitude he has taken? Or the hon. member for South Battle-ford, who is so eager to intervene in the debate?

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: I did not say a word. I was busy listening.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
My hon. friend has that
dark growl which percolates through the chamber. He will stand up and vote slavishly for a twelve year maintenance of a cent a pound on sugar, but he will oppose and criticise this government for doing precisely the same thing as was done by his own party when in power, the only difference being that the time limit in this case is five years instead of twelve.
I cannot understand my right hon. friend. Not only have we this action of his before us, but wa have him in imperial conferences proclaiming to the high heavens the very same general principle that the present Prime Minister sought to carry out in these agreements. He has given utterance to that in the old country and to the world from the public platform. I noticed a few minutes ago he was quite careful to correct some of his utterances by saying:	Of course we are in
favour of this family idea. He was not very much in favour of this family idea a few days ago, but since these damning quotations were read the other night he has thought it desirable to place himself a little more in line with his own utterances when he was in office and when he was over at the imperial conference. I invite him now to the penitents' bench; I invite him to put himself in line

Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
with himself when he was negotiating this treaty with the West Indies, to put himself somewhere measurably near his attitude when he had the responsibility of office, instead of putting himself where he is now, in bickering opposition to these things. Neither the right hon. gentleman nor those associated with him can find any reasonable fault with these agreements. I can understand some of my hon. friends in the far corner opposite, who hold strong free trade views, and the hon. member for Weyburn, who has wobbled very much on that question in recent years, taking objection to any of these things, but it does not lie in the mouths of hon. gentlemen directly opposite, who sit behind the right hon. leader of the opposition, who give their allegiance to him, to criticise this government, for its tariff policy, other than perhaps in ^ regard to some of the items; because in principle they are not at all apart from us in what we are doing here, and they will find it exceedingly difficult to hide their heads from justifiable attack in regard to the former utterances of their leader.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: Practically every argument advanced by hon. gentlemen opposite in reply to those presented from this side against the treaties has amounted to this, that in some past time the Liberal party did a similar thing. I am not greatly concerned about what the Liberal party may have done in past ages. I am more concerned about these agreements that are before us tonight. My hon. friend has just said that we, when we were in power, fixed a duty of one cent a pound on sugar for twelve years. My hon. friends opposite have increased it since they have come into office.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: May I interrupt my hon. friend? My officers have just checked the matter up and they tell me there has been no change since we have been in office.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: There is no change in the tariff schedule, but an order in council was passed fixing a value for duty on sugar. We raided the question in the house last session, and the Minister of National Revenue explained the situation in this way: that the beet growers of Canada came before him and told him that unless something was done to increase the duty on sugar they would not put in a crop.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
Not the duty on sugar It was to take care of the sugar that came from Cuba under circumstances which, as the hon. gentleman knows, were destroying not only the beet sugar industry here but the

West Indian sugar industry as well. It was to preserve the market we had promised them under the treaty as well as the beet sugar industry here that the order in council was passed dealing with Cuban sugar.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: The duty was raised by order in council.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: Not the duty.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: The value for duty was fixed, and so the duty was raised. The minister told us that that was done to encourage the farmers to sow beets, but what did he do? He raised the duty on refined sugar and left the duty on raw sugar where it was.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: That was covered by the treaty, and he could not change it. Surely the hon. gentleman knows that.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: Then what benefit was the beet grower going to get out of it? He was going to sell raw sugar.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: It kept Cuban sugar out.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
The beet growers went home thinking they were getting something, but my hon. friend raised the duty on refined sugar and left the duty on raw sugar where it was. Article 23 of the agreement between Canada and Great Britain reads:
In the event of circumstances arising which, in the judgment of His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom or of His Majesty's government in Canada, as the case may be, necessitate a variation in the terms of the agreement, the proposal to vary those terms shall form the subject of consultation between the two governments.
That is to say, if the governments of Canada and Great Britain are agreed that the agreement should be varied they can hold consultations and arrange to vary it, but there is no such provision for changing the South African agreement. If you will look at the schedules in the South African agreement, you will find that most of them read, preferential rate, preferential rate, preferential rate. The fact that this South African agreement will be in existence will nullify article 23 of the agreement between Canada and the motherland. Subsection 2 of article I of the South African agreement reads:
To enjoy the benefit of the tariff advantages provided for in section 1 of this article goods originating in and coming from the Union of South Africa shall be imported direct into Canada.
I take that to mean that unless the goods come direct from South Africa to Canada they will not enjoy these preferential rates but

South Africa
will come under the general rates. Am I right in that? I turn to the customs tariff of Canada, and appendix No. 1 reads:
The British preferential tariff shall apply to goods the produce or manufacture of the following countries

Then follows a long list of countries in which is included the Union of South Africa. Further down on the same page I read:
Provided, however, that goods entitled to the benefits of the British preferential tariff shall be accorded such benefits when such goods are shipped on a through bill of lading consigned to a consignee in a specified port in Canada when such goods are transferred at a port of a British colony or possession not enjoying the benefits of the British preferential tariff, and conveyed without further transhipment into a sea or river port of Canada.
That is to say, heretofore South Africa enjoyed the preferential rates. Now the rates in this schedule are mainly preferential rates. South Africa enjoyed them before, but she was allowed to ship her goods to England, transship them from there to Canada, and still get the benefit of the preferential rates; but that privilege is denied her in this agreement.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA

We will suffer. Further down I read this:
The importer of goods entitled to the benefits of the British preferential tariff shall be entitled to a discount of ten per centum on the amount of duty computed under such tariff, when such goods are conveyed without transhipment from a port of a country enjoying the benefits of the British preferential tariff into a sea, lake or river port of Canada.
That is to say, hitherto goods coming directly from South Africa to Canada paid ten per cent less than the preferential rate. Now, with that clause abolished and the goods required to come direct from South Africa to Canada to get the preference, they will not get the benefit of that ten per cent discount.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: Oh, no.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA

speechtext: My hon. friend is wrong.

speechtext:
He is right. These goods are not allowed to be transshipped under this
agreement. Hitherto if they came direct without being transshipped they got ten per cent below the preferential rate. The result is that the effect of this agreement has been to increase the duty on goods coming from South Africa to Canada by ten per cent.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: That is wrong.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: It is not. Read the section.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: I am very sorry, but my hon. friend is wrong.

speechtext:
It reads:
The importer of goods entitled to the benefits of the British preferential tariff shall be entitled to a discount of ten per centum on the amount of duty computed under such tariff, when such goods are conveyed without transhipment from a port of a country enjoying the benefits of the British preferential tariff into a sea, lake or river port of Canada.
When you look at the schedule of this agreement you will find that most of the rates are substantially the same as the preferential rate was before.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: If my hon. friend will permit me, the whole preferential is still enjoyed by South Africa.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
But subsection 2 of article I of the agreement between Canada and South Africa provides that unless the goods come direct to Canada they do not enjoy the rates set out in the agreement, and if they do not enjoy those rates they will pay the general rates. Surely that is plain enough; anybody can understand it. Most of the schedules are the same as the preferential rate. Why, then, make an agreement with South Africa fixing the duties at what they were without the treaty? The reason I believe is to be found in article IV of the agreement between Canada and South Africa. It reads:
His Majesty's government in the Dominion of Canada will, in regard to the goods enumerated in schedule A maintain the margins of tariff concessions represented by the difference between the rates accorded to Union goods in that schedule and the presently existing rates on similar goods when imported from any foreign country.
That is to say, this agreement does not lower the duties on goods coming from South Africa; it simply agrees not to lower the duties on goods coming from anywhere else. We have raised the duty on goods coming from South Africa by ten per cent, and we are agreeing not to lower them against any other country.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
I am sorry to have to take any part in this debate, but I have been drawn into it by the reference made to sugar.

Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
The situation in regard to sugar was this. There was a very important sugar manufacturing industry at Wallaceburg, also at Chatham. Six thousand farmers enjoy the privilege, so long as it is offered to them, of furnishing sugar beets to this factory. It is an important factor in the life of everyone who lives in that district, and anyone who knows anything about the industry is well informed with regard to it. Remember that there are three points at which those who seek to attack our sugar market in Central Canada may do so. There is Windsor, and next Toronto, and farther east, Montreal. This factory at Wallaceburg said: We want to help those six thousand farmers and we want to take care of all the sugar beets with which they can supply us, but owing to the transportation situation, refined sugar can be landed in Toronto at a rate which we cannot beat because of the dumping; they do not take account of the transportation charges, and in order to kill us in the western part of Ontario they are furnishing sugar at such and such a price. Notwithstanding what may be said on the other side of the house, this government was sincerely anxious that those six thousand farmers, and it may be a much greater number than that, should get the benefit of the sugar beet industry. The company undertook that it would not raise the price of sugar, so what we did was simply to step in and fix the value for sugar, and to tell those who wanted to knock off the freight rate and dump their sugar on the market to go east and west, that they could not do it. The action was taken in the interest of the farmers, and, I submit in the interest of all Canadian trade.

speechtext: Was it on refined or raw sugar?

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: Refined.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: Precisely.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
Now that I am on my feet I should like to address my remarks to one argument concerning this or any other of the agreements. These trade arrangements were reached through negotiations. In this instance the conclusions were satisfactory to the representatives of South Africa, and the representatives from the United Kingdom were satisfied with their agreement. The agreements were bilateral, such as one government might enter into with a neighbouring government. In such case one's neighbour may be satisfied with the way he has been treated, and you may be satisfied with the way he has treated you. Why waste the time of the house dealing with these matters? Investigate them, surely; but these are agree-

ments reached by men of equal ability-let me put it that way-by men with ability equal to that of any hon. member in the house. The agreements represent their bargaining as well as ours. Why inveigh against us? Why suggest that the whole responsibility for the agreements and the results flowing from them depend upon the party on this side of the house? In our dominions there are parliaments whose representatives sat with us. Those men-Olympic men, may I say-did their share in framing the agreements, and I suggest that when hon. members opposite criticize us they are inveighing against the representatives of other parts of the empire who agreed that the deliberations in Ottawa were in their own interests as well as ours. If they were satisfied that their interests were helped by the agreements at the conference, surely it is fair to say that they did not, as has been suggested in this house, throw into the air all rights and benefits accruing to them from constitutional law and the like. They are just as anxious to maintain the dignity of the component parts of the British Empire as are any hon. members in this chamber. When accusations are lodged against the party on this side of the house I should like the accusers to bear in mind that these agreements were entered into after thorough discussion, and I resent the idea that there was anything in the nature of coercion. It was my privilege to be a delegate, and as such I believe I saw what was taking place.
I have been pained to hear the allegations that coercion took place, and the suggestion that there were unseemly arguments. I heard nothing of the kind. Remember that these agreements have been reached after deliberations between men sitting in this house and others from beyond the seas, men who were just as anxious to work for the benefit of their countries as we were to work in the interests of ours. I suggest it is not fair to pillory this side of the house alone and to state the intention of overturning the agreements, because these agreements were concluded only after deliberations with men who are not now here but who worked in concert with us.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
I do not wish to take the time of the committee for more than a moment or two, but I do not think the Minister of National Revenue should be impatient and talk about what he has termed a waste of time. We must remember that these agreements are important, and have been so regarded by the government. The country, the press and the public generally have followed their history, and aLl people have been interested in the results of the conference. I feel therefore that we ought to be forgiven if, not as olympians, but as ordinary individuals we try to find out what is in them, and subject them to the scrutiny prompted by our sense of duty, so that we may discharge our responsibilities as legislators.
The minister has mentioned that other, men in other countries have been parties to the agreements, and has suggested that in criticizing Canadian representatives at the conference we are criticizing people in other countries. I want him and the committee to remember that there is a vast difference between the agreement made by representatives from the United Kingdom and that made by the Canadian representatives. Within the last few days we have been shown very forcibly that while we may have made an agreement which binds us solidly for five years, men on the other side of the Atlantic, with regard to the long list of articles to which the Prime Minister referred in his speech when introducing the resolution, consider themselves free to change their duties as they see fit. They allege they are not bound for five years, and therefore I submit they are not open to the criticism which may properly be levelled at the heads of hon. members opposite. That is the first difference between the agreement as it applies to us and as it applies to other countries. My suggestion is that that constitutes one of the essential points of criticism. When we look at the United Kingdom agreement as defined in Great Britain and find that we receive only free entry, but no agreement that the duties are to be kept up or imposed against the rest of the world, and compare with that our agreement which provides that the margin of preference shall be maintained, and that the present tariff rates on one hundred and fifty-nine articles are to be pegged for five years, we immediately realize the difference.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has invited criticism, I submit I have made a valid objection, and one which has received considerable attention in Canada. My hon. friends opposite have tried to slur over the suggestion that Great Britain was not bound. The statement was made in the British house only a few days ago that Great Britain is not bound for five years, but we are. The committee and country may as well get that idea into their minds.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: I know the hon. member does not wish to be unfair; he has invited me to state the matter clearly. The Union of South Africa is bound precisely the same as the Dominion of Canada.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
Yes, but I am answering the argument made by the Minister of National Revenue and by the Prime Minister, who talked about family agreements. The agreement with South Africa is merely a side issue; the five year term there may not mean much one way or the other. Hon. members opposite are always impressing upon us the fact that they have made some splendid agreement with the United Kingdom and that when we criticize this government we are criticizing gentlemen on the other side of the ocean. I am pointing out that there is good ground for criticism of our representatives who have made an agreement binding us for five years, but have not required the same preference in our favour.
The other objection is this: What we have tried to say and what we will continue to say is that the very spirit of economic and fiscal relations within the last year or two years has been towards lower tariffs. And you will find as late as last month, October of this year, the report of the Bank of Nova Scotia again reiterates that the world-wide isolation by means of tariffs is one of the things which is causing the present difficulties and preventing the return of prosperity. We hoped and believed, the world hoped, and I am sure Canada hoped, that this conference would have been the beginning of a lowering of tariffs. Mr. Baldwin in his opening address made it very clear that he expected and hoped that preferences would be reached by lowering tariffs and not by raising them. The point we are making, and that is not, and I think cannot be answered by the other side, is that on nearly one hundred and fifty -items of the United Kingdom agreement-I cannot tell how many in this, because I have not examined it-on nearly one hundred and fifty items the tariffs have been raised. And instead of having freedom of action we have a higher tariff nailed on Canada than has ever been

there before. That is one of the differences between this and the West Indies agreement- and I commend it to the Minister of Trade and Commerce-the West Indies agreement in general did not raise tariffs, but in the United Kingdom agreement tariffs have been raised on nearly one hundred and fifty items in our schedule in order that a preference might be given. And this at a time when the tendency of the world in regard to tariffs-and everyone is talking about it, not only economists, who were rather sneered at by the Prime Minister the other night-

Yet in face of that this conference is held and Canada emerges with an added tariff on nearly one hundred and fifty items, and that tariff riveted on us for five years. That I submit is an objection which is fundamental and goes to the very root of these agreements. That is why we are taking the time, in spite of what my hon. friend the Minister of National Revenue, said to impress that on our friends opposite and on the country generally.
My right hon. friend the Prime Minister says it is necessary to have stability, so we must have this for five years. I asked him then why did not the statesmen from Great Britain, -the men from Olympus as they were referred to by my hon. friend the Minister of National Revenue-give us a five year preference and stabilize our trade relations?

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA

speechtext: I should like to ask the Prime Minister a question with regard to the bearing of these tariff rates upon anything that may transpire at the forthcoming world economic conference. My right hon. friend will recall having mentioned that the conference was to be held this year, but apparently they are debating now whether it can be held before next summer. However, when the conference does meet, will the fact that Canada has agreed to maintain certain of its tariffs at a certain figure in any way prejudice the freedom of that conference to declare in favour of the rescission of all tariffs, say, if they wished to go that far?

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
I rather think the right hon. gentleman is not serious in asking that question. What he asked as to the world economic conference was a perfectly sound question, though I do not know whether or not it touches this agreement. The truth is

that when the matter was under debate in the house the agenda was being considered, and at that time it was thought that the date of the conference would be fixed for some time this month. I dare say the right hon. gentleman has seen what the Prime Minister of Great Britain said the other day with regard to the delay in settling the agenda, which was being looked after at Geneva. I assume that all the countries concerned will be represented at the world economic conference, and if a situation arises where it is felt desirable that there should be any abrogation, by consent, of agreements that have been entered into not only between Great Britain and the dominions but between Great Britain and foreign countries, or trade agreements between foreign countries that have nothing to do with us, I assume if it is agreed that it is desirable and in the interests of the various countries that such abrogation should be brought about there is nothing to prevent its being done. But obviously, I say, the right hon. gentleman is not serious in asking the question he has directed to me, for despite the great appreciation that he concedes me with regard to these matters-which I imagine is more illusory than real-I am not in a position to answer that question. I very much regret it.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: My right hon. friend can answer it so far as Canada is concerned. As he knows, the world economic conference is being called for the purpose of helping to remove some of the restrictions to trade. That is one of the main purposes of the conference, to see what can be done in that regard.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: I do not think that is definitely stated.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: The consideration of tariff barriers, or the equivalent, is one of the questions to come before the conference- At any rate, if the -conference is not called for the purpose of helping to remove restrictions to trade, I do not see what possible service a world economic conference could render at this time, because the world must look to greater freedom of trade between nations. Surely my right hon. friend can answer this question, as to whether in his opinion he, as the leader of the government in this country, apart from all the other countries, would feel that these agreements in any way restricted his freedom in the matter of declaring for or against the abolition of the tariff or any -particular commodity that might be mentioned in the agreements.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
That is a very simple
question to answer, Mr. Chairman. If I had to consider the question of sugar, for example, I would realize at once that the contract or agreement which the right hon. gentleman entered into prevented me from dealing with that matter. Therefore I could not deal with it. I would be bound in honour to respect the agreements of Canada, and if I had to deal with other countries with which we have outstanding contracts or agreements I would be bound by the same considerations. Unless the parties to the agreement consented to abrogate such agreement and terminate their rights I would have to be bound by that agreement. That is particularly so with respect to many items covered by contracts made before we came into office. We are equally bound by those we made after we came into office as by those which were made before. We will respect the obligations of Canada, because Canada is not a matter of political parties. We will respect the obligations of this dominion whether they were entered into by hon. gentlemen opposite or by ourselves; it matters not.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: My hon. friend speaks of agreements which existed before he came into office and of others which were made later. maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA

They can take care of themselves. They always have done so and I believe they always will do so. maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
Very well; I will sum up my remarks in this way. Without discussing this item in particular, I sincerely believe the government-I am speaking in a general way -was within its right to make trade agreements with the Union of South Africa, Southern Rhodesia and the Irish Free State, because it was a matter of nation dealing with nation. Relations between nations may be likened to those between individuals, and this is why, without discussing each item in particular, my idea is that the only way to make treaties is to bind one nation to another nation and not for several nations or dominions to sign a treaty or different treaties at the same time and under the same circumstances with one particular nation. When this occurs it is no longer a treaty, it is an auction, and in that auction each one is to be treated in the same way. I quite understand that there should be imperial political conferences
that have for their aim to give a certain status or certain political rights to all the dominions and to each of them. But when the matter becomes one of trade, it is entirely different, because there must be competition between those dominions which have similar products to offer to the mother country or to another dominion. In this instance we have to consider not only this treaty between the Dominion of Canada and the Union of South Africa, but also the treaty that has been passed between the Dominion of Canada and the United Kingdom. This is why I say that if I approve, not the general lines but the drafting of this treaty between the Dominion of Canada and the Union of South Africa, I cannot understand how the Dominion of Canada has agreed to meet with the other dominions in order to get some advantages from Britain, because in each case when an advantage was given to one of the dominions which had sent delegates here, the same advantage was given to each one. No one could get more than another, and they all receive the same treatment on the British market.

speechtext: There are about fifty items in schedule A and I notice most of them receive the British preferential rate. speechtext:
If my hon friend will
recall, this afternoon I tried to explain the policy of the Union of South Africa in dealing with their tariff. It is somewhat different from that of any of the other dominions. They give to one country a list of privileges, shall I say, that is usually limited to that country. Some of them may be extended as in this case to Great Britain, but not to the other dominions. Then they would give to another dominion privileges on a list of articles that in all probability would not be extended to the Dominion of Canada, but the list is selected as that most satisfactory to both parties. Such is the case in this agreement. But when we were fixing the rates of duty it was thought desirable and acceptable to them to put in "British preferential rate" in many cases instead of specifying a certain rate. That method leaves it free to change the item according to the change in the British preferential rate. In other words, as long as they got the British preferential rate, they were satisfied. Does that answer my hon. friend's question?

speechtext: We agreed with the South African delegation before they left here that we would follow our usual practice in these matters, and we agreed similarly with the others as well, that when the tariff items were introduced in the form of resolutions they would contain the usual clause as heretofore.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
This act does not go into force until a date yet to be agreed upon, as I read it, and I was going to ask the Prime Minister, at the risk of again meeting with a refusal, if he would not agree with South Africa to wait until after the world economic conference before putting this agreement into effect. But that is a separate question.
I do submit that there is no authority whatever for the tariff changes proposed in this schedule being in force at the present time. This parliament has not yet approved this agreement, and yet we are told that these particular schedules are in force. In other words, taxation is being imposed upon the people of this country without the consent of parliament, and notwithstanding that the language of the agreement expressly provides that these duties shall not be imposed until a date yet to be agreed upon between the two governments. The general language which the Prime Minister has used in reply does not at all meet the situation. There may be parliamentary procedure regulating how certain rates are to go into effect, but when an agreement expressly provides that it shall not go into effect until a date yet to be agreed upon no portion of that agreement should be in force until that time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext: I am sorry that my right hon. friend has not followed me. We have introduced certain resolutions which are now before the ways and means committee. The last budget that was introduced into this house by the Minister of Finance was introduced in exactly the same way, and the schedules became operative from the day the resolutions were laid on the table. This agreement as such will become operative upon proclamation, but the rates having been agreed upon and put into force as I have indicated, are now in force just as under the Dunning budget so-called the resolutions became effective and telegrams were sent to every collector of customs accordingly on the evening of the delivery of the budget. These items before us, in accordance with our arrangements, are being treated in exactly the same way and are being acted upon accordingly.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
I contend that it is wholly irregular. A budget is one thing and an agreement of this character is another. The tariff changes proposed in a budget as everyone knows, go into force the moment the tariff resolutions referred to therein are tabled. But here is a specific agreement which, according to its own terms, does not go into force until a date still to be agreed upon. There is the distinction between the two, a distinction which ought to have been taken notice of. May I draw attention to the difference between the agreement entered into between the United Kingdom and Canada and this agreement? The agreement with the United Kingdom went into effect on the date it was signed, August 20, 1932, but this agreement does not go into force until a date still to be agreed upon. In those two particulars

The point is that the
Union of South Africa did propose in some cases to pay a bonus on certain primary products when exported. This country, in common with other countries, has looked askance on goods imported into Canada under a bonus. It is felt that they do not permit of fair competition. As a matter of fact corn exported from South Africa to Canada was never bonused, because the South African government and South African exporters knew that Canada had provision for the imposition of a dump on bonused imports. They did not pay the bonus in order that the dump might not apply, and for that reason the dump was not applied. This matter was discussed fully with South African representatives and they agreed frankly it would not be fair to Canadian corn producers to have bonused com enter the market in competition with our own home-grown product. They have agreed therefore that no bonus will be paid, and in order that we may have a check it is provided that the invoices of the com when landed in Canada must show a price of not less than the

It is only what is sold on the market that will come into competition with imported com.

maintopic: TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNION OF SOUTH AFRICA
speechtext:
That is a question to which a good deal of study has been given recently. Com happens to be a farm product that is perhaps the most difficult of the major productions to check and keep track of. The reason is that most of the com is produced in western Canada and there are not adequate public warehouse facilities and drying plants to take care of it. Consequently it is not accumulated in large quantities like other grains such as wheat, oats, and barley, and it is rather difficult to keep track of its movement anl the manner in which it finds its way to market. But there is no doubt that a very substantial portion of that com is fed. My hon. friend must remember that the major uses for which corn is imported are, I would say, first for distillation purposes, second for the manufacture of starch and other products of that general character, syrup, cornmeal and so on; and third, in some sections of the country, particularly the maritime provinces and the seaboard, for feed. Now it will be clear to my 'hon. friend that to move com say from western Ontario to the maritimes is difficult in competition with seaborne traffic. The consequence is, I imagine, that the bulk of the com used in the maritime provinces and eastern seaboard, as well as the western seaboard, is imported com. Of course it would be impossible

to transport com from western Ontario to British Columbia, so that a considerable quantity is imported. Up to a year ago, or within the last year, the major portion of this corn came from the United States, and some from the Argentine. But by the imposition of certain tariff provisions this business has tea large extent been diverted to South Africa, and South Africa and Rhodesia will undoubtedly be the major sources of supply of corn imported into this country.

speechtext:

I believe that bill is printed in both English and French, ready for distribution if we can reach it. I suppose there is no chance of finishing it to-morrow, but if we should do so we will take up the other items on the order paper.

Including the amendment to the Customs Act and the representation bill, before we go into committee of ways and means. If it suits the purpose of my right hon. friend not to discuss the bill at great length, assuming as I do that he and his party are opposed to it, we will be able

to go into committee of ways and means and enter into what I suppose will be the more lengthy discussion of the two.
I had thought of moving the representation bill at the proper time but I did not intend to do more than move the second reading, together with a resolution that it be referred to a committee, which might be named either before or after adjournment as the house thinks best. The right hon. gentleman will remember that in 1923 the motion was that the bill be referred to a committee, and later the committee was named by resolution which does not require notice. I will pursue either course as the right hon. gentleman and his friends desire. I thought we might give the bill second reading and provide for its reference to a committee; then the committee could be named now or when the house reconvenes as may be thought best. It did occur to me personally, however, that it might be desirable to set up the committee so that during the recess the individual members might have an opportunity to consider the question from the various standpoints from which they think it should be considered in order to enable them to arrive at a report. If during the next day or two the right hon. gentleman has an opportunity to consider the question I shall bo glad to meet his wishes in that regard.
